title: canvas-widgets: no canvas::Cache anywhere - every widget re-tessellates every frame
notes:
VERIFIED TODAY, not inferred: `grep -rn --include='*.rs' -E "canvas::Cache|Cache::new|\.cache\.draw" crates/`
returns NOTHING across the whole workspace, against 19 bare `Frame::new` call sites (11 in
canvas-widgets, 8 in canvas). There are 10 `impl canvas::Program` blocks in live.rs alone
(1243, 1308, 1358, 1409, 1470, 1668, 1706, 1742, 1787, 1896).

CONSEQUENCE: every widget fully re-tessellates its geometry on every repaint. On a 5760x1200 wall
with the whole fleet view up, that is the entire scene rebuilt per frame for data that did not
change. This is very likely the largest single performance defect in the renderer.

THE FIX IS ALREADY COMPILED IN. `canvas::Cache` ships in iced_widget 0.14.2 - `cache.draw(renderer,
size, |frame| ...)` re-runs the closure only when the cache is cleared. Zero new dependencies. The
work is: give each Program a Cache, key it on the data it draws, and clear on change. It applies to
all ten programs including Gauge, StateTimeline and SloBurnRate.

This finding came out of the charting-dependency evaluation (docs/charting-dependency-decision.md),
which concluded that the two changes that would most improve the wall are both ALREADY IN THE
BINARY - this one and iced::Animation - and that no charting crate was worth adopting. Do this one
first: it is also the honest test of whether the renderer is slow because of what it draws or
because of how often it redraws it.
PRIORITISED BY AVERY 2026-09-10: "The Cache finding is huge and should be prioritized." Raised P1 ->
P0. It is the cheapest large win available - no new dependency, no design decision, no interface
change - and it is upstream of judging anything else about renderer performance. Do it before
anyone measures whether the wall is slow because of WHAT it draws.
close_reason: Closed

title: Canvas leaks presence: unredacted roster to every caller, no test guards it
notes:
VERIFIED IN SHIPPED CODE 2026-09-09. Found by design analysis, then each claim confirmed by reading the file.

1. crates/canvas/src/main.rs:3404 - presence: self.presence.clone(). One global slot is echoed
   wholesale into RuntimeSnapshot, so every control reply and the MCP echo ship the full occupant
   roster to every loopback caller, unredacted and unscoped.
2. NO TEST ANYWHERE asserts that stale or unknown presence stops a name being drawn. A grep for
   stale_presence / unidentified_occupant returns nothing across all crates.
3. crates/canvas/src/main.rs:~7648 asserts the OPPOSITE property - that a presence snapshot
   round-trips through Canvas unchanged. There is a test actively defending the leak.
4. crates/canvas/src/main.rs:4980-4984 overlay_on_viewport uses is_none_or, which is TRUE when the
   option is None, so an unresolved display satisfies the predicate and the overlay draws
   EVERYWHERE. It fails open.
5. jarvis-presence/src/canvas.rs:221,226 emits unknown-{index} and an Unknown person label, so an
   unidentified person in the room becomes a roster entry rather than being omitted.

THE ASYMMETRY IS CANVAS-SIDE ONLY. JARVIS tests the correct narrowing three times over -
identity.rs:514-532, tact.rs:111-160, publication.rs:202-204 - and jarvis/distributed-topology.md
states the rule plainly: a face observation alone must not silently give an unknown speaker another
person's private history. The brain gets this right; the workbench does not.

FIX, per docs/coordinator-and-scope.md, and it is the recommended first move under every proposal
the design considered:
- Replace self.presence.clone() with assemble_presence(viewer, observation, now) - per-caller
  assembly rather than a shared clone.
- EMPTY rather than mark on expiry. Those semantics are already proven at
  jarvis-presence/src/publication.rs:96-104.
- Omit any occupant whose identity is not currently verified, instead of emitting an unknown-N row.
- Fix the is_none_or branches to fail closed: unresolved display identity means the overlay draws
  NOWHERE.
- Invert the round-trip test, and add the two tests that do not exist:
  stale_presence_draws_no_name and unidentified_occupant_draws_no_name.

Touches no storage format, no transport and no wire schema - the field's type is unchanged, so
deny_unknown_fields and the schema_version check are undisturbed. Required regardless of how the
coordinator question is answered.
close_reason: Closed

title: Mount shared views and couple capture to displayed state
description: Integrate SharedViewDocument into the Canvas runtime, surfaces, control socket and MCP so an agent and human operate on the same mounted view. Image/PDF viewports and attention must render visibly; captures must identify and use the exact displayed view revision and source positions.
acceptance_criteria: Canvas can open and inspect a shared image view, atomically patch its viewport/attention, visibly render the result, and capture the same view revision; human pan/zoom updates the document; MCP schemas and receipts expose exact view and source revisions; tests reject stale or mismatched capture requests.
notes:
2026-09-08 slice: image/PDF loads now mount SharedViewDocument state; control/MCP inspect exposes visible absolute surface bounds and exact view/source revisions; canvas_view_patch visibly applies normalized GPU crop and attention; canvas_view_capture validates runtime+view revisions, captures only the resolved surface, returns metadata+PNG, and re-inspects after readback to reject concurrent changes. Generic surface screenshots now use surface bounds. Full workspace build/test/clippy/fmt passed. Remaining before close: direct human pan/zoom must mutate the same view. Display-independent offscreen/headless GPU capture is tracked by dock-cov.12.
Live macOS smoke testing exposed a compositor false positive: screencapture returned bare wallpaper while runtime state still identified the requested surface. Surface capture now verifies the existing Canvas traffic-light chrome using runtime theme colors and fails loudly when pixels are occluded or come from another Space. MCP capture remains passive and never shows, focuses, or rearranges Canvas. Reliable occlusion-independent capture remains dock-cov.12.
Direct local MCP setup verified 2026-09-08: installed matching dock-canvas/dock-canvas-mcp binaries without launching or focusing Canvas, retained the FPL Desktop Bridge dock-canvas connector, registered ~/.local/bin/dock-canvas-mcp globally in Codex as dock-canvas, negotiated MCP 2025-06-18, listed all 15 tools, and completed a read-only canvas_inspect call.
Live direct MCP joyride: relaunched the matching runtime, opened docs/screenshots/dock-dark.png as joyride-dock on the right display, inspected its exact bounds and SharedViewDocument revision, then patched viewport plus agent attention from view revision 1 to 2 with a successful revisioned receipt. macOS screencapture still omits the on-screen Metal host window and returns the pixels beneath it; the capture guard correctly rejects the result. title: Define joint artifact and view-state contract
description: Specify and implement the versioned boundary that lets Canvas, a human, and an agent refer to the same visual thing and the same exact view of it. Cover finite artifacts and live sources without coupling the document to SSE, inbox, filesystem, camera, or model-provider details.
design: Model source identity/provenance separately from ViewState. A view owns normalized viewport, optional selection/annotation, page or playhead, filters and source revision. All mutations use optimistic revisions. Capture/inspection must name the resulting view revision so an agent cannot silently inspect pixels different from what Canvas shows.
acceptance_criteria: Rust types validate source references, provenance and bounded shared view state; patches can focus a normalized image region without replacing the artifact; serialization is MCP-schema-compatible; tests cover invalid bounds, stale revisions and a finite image plus a live graph source; the architecture document gives a manual runbook from source resolution to shared display and inspection.
notes: Implemented dock_canvas::view contract with keyed multi-source bindings, artifact/live source positions, normalized viewport, visible attention ownership, page/timeline navigation, typed parameters, and atomic revision-checked patches. Tests prove image-region focus preserves artifact identity, two live sources share one view lifecycle, invalid regions/source modes fail, stale patches conflict, and JSON round-trips. Added architecture boundary and manual runbook; repaired existing all-feature mlua callback/table integration exposed by the gate.
close_reason: The shared multi-source artifact/view-state contract, validation, patch semantics, tests, architecture document, and runbook are implemented.

title: Make Canvas the shared human-agent visualization plane
description: Canvas is the common visualization layer for static artifacts and live data, and the joint visual context shared by a human and AI. Any authorized source can publish typed data or references; deterministic reducers and capability-scoped Lua map them into views; both parties observe and change the same revisioned view state instead of maintaining separate chat and screen representations.
design: Separate immutable or owner-referenced artifacts from mutable joint view state. Normalize finite snapshots and unbounded streams behind one typed source contract. Keep transport, authorization, decoding and rendering outside Lua; Lua adapts bounded typed inputs into retained visual scenes. MCP expresses intent and reads exact state; the owner-local socket applies deterministic revisioned transitions. View state includes viewport, selection, page/playhead, filters, presentation and provenance so agent inspection is visibly mirrored on Canvas.
acceptance_criteria: An agent can publish or resolve an artifact/data source, open a shared view, focus or annotate the exact region it is inspecting, and capture that same view revision; human interactions update the state the agent reads; one streaming source and one finite artifact use the same lifecycle; a Lua adapter can render a bounded unfamiliar graph stream without owning I/O; provenance and authorization remain inspectable.
notes: 2026-09-08 product direction: Canvas is the shared view/window manager for human-AI collaboration and the common view language for all signals. Reference workloads include Elmer's brain and MCP firing SSE graphs, Edgerunner DAGs, Prometheus instruments, Panopticon maps, trading/mixed-export analysis, presence, terminals/NVR/media, STL/STEP/wireframe/FEA/CAM/microscope, Gaussian splats/RuView/PolyLayout, music visualizers, generated CSV+Lua/template explanations, Maxim-style narratives and future XR. Preserve steering/observability and hands-on engineering/vibe-coding as equal modes. Alfalfa owns identity/workflow/admin; JARVIS owns voice/presence; domain systems own data/actions/hardware; Canvas owns shared views/layout/capture/presentation. Portable state uses compact JSON snapshots plus JSONL patch/receipt journals; Lua owns bounded presentation logic.

title: Configure Canvas overlays and global visibility
description: The shared multi-display Canvas currently repeats overlays per host window, the compact presence indicator does not provide JARVIS's working live tray behavior, and there is no global way to reveal the underlying macOS desktop. Add deterministic display anchors for overlays, place the live presence rail on the bottom-left/leftmost selected display, place the Conky HUD on the rightmost selected display, preserve Lua as a client of the runtime configuration interface, and register a global Mac shortcut that atomically shows or hides every Canvas host window.
acceptance_criteria: Presence rail updates live and renders only on the leftmost selected display; Conky HUD renders only on the rightmost selected display; socket state/configuration represents overlay anchors without duplicating placement logic in Lua; a documented global Mac shortcut hides and restores all selected Canvas windows together; tests cover viewport anchors and visibility state transitions; live three-monitor verification succeeds.
notes: 2026-09-08 implemented and deployed: typed OverlaySettings via raw socket and MCP; defaults place live JARVIS rail/preview on leftmost, HUD on rightmost, FPL mark leftmost, compact orb hidden, shortcut help centered. Ctrl-Option-C globally hides/restores all native Canvas windows while retaining daemon state; Ctrl-Option-? globally opens Help; plain ? opens Help only after a Canvas background click; Ctrl-Up/Down cycles exact project workspaces; Ctrl-Option-J toggles JARVIS presentation. Rebuilt the existing JARVIS Presence app after its packaged binary had been cleaned, restarted its owner LaunchAgent, and proved current presence reaches Canvas. Live proof: three selected 1920x1200 displays, shared 5760x1200 frame, static aurora-drift speed 0, visibility false then true, shortcut_help shown, presence live. Full workspace build/test/strict Clippy/format pass.
close_reason: Overlay placement, live presence restoration, shortcut help, and global three-window visibility toggle are implemented, tested, deployed, and live-verified.

title: Present Canvas as one shared desktop across displays
description: A single oversized native Canvas window records a multi-display frame but macOS separate Spaces prevents reliable presentation across the physical displays. Present one host window per selected display while retaining one WorkspaceDocument, one global z-order, and one virtual coordinate space so surfaces can be dragged across seams.
design: Add a renderer-neutral display topology and virtual-to-local projection boundary. The shell owns one borderless window per display and renders/clips the shared document through each display viewport. Pointer events translate from host-window local coordinates into virtual desktop coordinates before using the existing interaction engine. Monitor assignment remains host-local and socket/MCP driven.
acceptance_criteria: On the current three-display Mac, Canvas visibly covers each selected display; a surface can be dragged across both seams while preserving size, focus, and z-order; disconnect/reconnect and nonzero/negative origins fail or reconcile deterministically; socket inspection exposes selected display targets; tests cover topology, projection, and cross-display pointer translation.
notes: 2026-09-08 shared desktop slice implemented: one native host window per selected display over one WorkspaceDocument/global z-order/virtual frame; window-local pointer coordinates project to shared coordinates; display target exposed through socket and Canvas MCP; tests cover negative origins, seam projection, topology validation and second-display pointer translation. Live three-display 5760x1200 presentation verified by user and visibility hotkey proof. Remaining before closing: respond to display topology changes at runtime and prove disconnect/reconnect reconciliation without restarting Canvas.

title: Materialize and recover the managed Canvas native window
description: The managed dock-canvas process can own its socket, restore its full project WorkspaceDocument, and report connected displays while macOS exposes no native window. Focus is then a no-op because App.window remains unset. Closing or relaunching must recreate the desktop presentation instead of leaving a headless control process.
acceptance_criteria: Fresh LaunchAgent start creates one borderless Canvas window on the resolved display target; closing or losing that window either recreates it or terminates the runtime so supervision restarts it; focus brings it to the active Space; inspect distinguishes document state from presentation-window state; a live screenshot proves the restored Dock project desktop is visible after restart.
notes: 2026-09-07 slice cfdd1a0 replaces implicit oldest-window lookup with an explicit iced daemon window open, retains the exact returned window ID, and tests persistent borderless desktop settings. Deployed LaunchAgent restores dock with surfaces=1 and CoreGraphics proves one on-screen 1920x1200 window at 3840,0. Remaining: sharing state is still 0, so screencapture omits Canvas; inspect must report window presentation state and close/recovery needs a live proof.

title: Stop Canvas background flicker and expose frame pacing
description: The animated Canvas background flickers severely in the live desktop. Make shader animation opt-in while unstable, schedule generation at a bounded cadence, measure generated/presented cadence over a rolling interval, and expose a small configurable FPS diagnostic so frame pacing can be verified before deployment.
design: Keep timing deterministic in the Canvas runtime. Separate tick cadence, expensive shader generation cadence, and diagnostic sampling. Do not perform synchronous GPU readback unless animated background state explicitly enables it.
acceptance_criteria: The default Canvas launch is visually stable. Shader frames are never generated faster than the configured cap. A socket-controlled FPS overlay reports measured cadence. Tests cover disabled/default scheduling, capped scheduling, and meter calculation. The live right-monitor instance is verified without flicker.
notes: Implemented 2026-09-07: replaced synchronous wgpu readback plus per-frame iced image-handle allocation with an iced-native retained GPU shader primitive. Screensaver state is explicit over the socket, defaults disabled, validates 1-60 FPS, and optionally shows measured/target FPS. A deadline-based FrameClock bounds updates without accumulating timer drift. Live managed binary on right display measures 15.01 FPS at a 15 FPS target, CPU ~8%, RSS held 77.7-77.9 MiB over 10 seconds. Found and killed unmanaged target/debug processes that were stealing the socket from the LaunchAgent. 76 Canvas tests pass and strict all-target Clippy passes. Awaiting subjective confirmation that the display is visually calm before closing.
close_reason: Replaced the flickering readback path with retained GPU rendering, removed per-frame image allocation, added bounded deterministic pacing and optional FPS diagnostics, added compile-time WGSL parsing, eliminated duplicate unmanaged runtimes, and verified the managed right-display instance at ~15 FPS with stable RSS.

title: Render Panopticon intelligence as a native Canvas map
description: Add a first-class renderer-neutral map surface and native Canvas adapter. Canvas owns camera state, map interaction, transition timing, reduced-motion behavior, and compositing; it consumes authorized opaque map resources and never stores credentials or asks Panopticon to dictate pixels. Resolve natural-language place names outside the renderer into exact versioned geographic extents, then apply deterministic camera intents. Use a proven map engine through an offscreen texture boundary rather than implementing tile layout, labels, collision, and camera flight from scratch.
design: Define maps.viewport.v1 with target variants extent, center_zoom, entity, and current_results; WGS84 antimeridian-safe bounds; padding; bearing/pitch; and a renderer hint transition of jump, ease, or fly with bounded duration. Derive center/zoom from extent plus actual surface size instead of storing redundant values. Add a Map surface/resource binding to the WorkspaceDocument and revisioned patch protocol. Prototype MapLibre Native FFI owned-texture or borrowed-texture compositing on macOS Metal, keeping network/tile parsing off the iced render thread. The MCP path accepts an already-resolved extent or stable place reference; an orchestrator may resolve a phrase through Panopticon before issuing one exact Canvas mutation. Ambiguity must return candidates, never silently choose Springfield/Fremont. Preserve human gestures and cancel/retarget an in-flight agent animation deterministically.
acceptance_criteria: From one MCP-driven request, Canvas can show and smoothly fly between world, Seattle, Fremont Seattle, Manhattan, the five boroughs, and the NY/NJ/CT tri-state extent; fit current query results; and follow an entity. Camera movement is smooth on reference hardware, interruptible by direct human input, honors reduced motion, and does not mutate the durable document every frame. Retina output is sharp, labels do not visibly reflow after settling, stale tile/data failures are explicit, and credentials/endpoints never appear in the document or MCP receipt. Unit tests cover extent fitting, antimeridian bounds, ambiguity, revision conflicts, duration bounds, and transition cancellation; a live visual test records frame-time and command-to-first-motion latency.
notes:
Backend-first slice implemented locally without selecting a permanent engine: added a generic typed VisualBackend lifecycle with shared mount/update/resize/input/event/render/suspend/unmount semantics, revision enforcement, reduced-motion context, retained-frame outcomes, and adapter-neutral errors. Added maps.viewport model types with opaque resource identity, semantic layers, extent/center/follow/fit targets, antimeridian-safe bounds, provenance refs, surface-derived Web Mercator camera fitting, bounded jump/ease/fly transitions, and reduced-motion resolution. Validation on 2026-09-07 used /Volumes/DOC MOVIES/dock-cargo-target because the local disk filled: all 48 dock-canvas all-feature library tests pass and strict all-feature library Clippy with -D warnings passes. Focused rustfmt is clean. Concurrent Canvas work remains in the shared worktree and was preserved. Remaining on this feature: put MapSurface into the WorkspaceDocument after current document work settles, implement the MapLibre FFI texture adapter behind VisualBackend, wire map gestures/animation interruption, add map-specific MCP convenience operations, and perform native visual/performance proof.
2026-09-07 renderer direction: native-first Rust + Lua + wgpu/WGSL. Do not introduce deck.gl or a large JavaScript visualization runtime. MapLibre Native may remain a bounded C++/FFI map backend behind VisualBackend; Canvas owns the Rust compositor and MCP surface. Treat browser rendering as a thin fallback or a build from the shared typed scene contract, not the source of truth.
Wishlist extension from the operational-view audit: native map presentation should also compose trip-planning views for sailing and camping—route, waypoints, scale/bearing, weather, tides/currents, hazards and contact cards—while Panopticon and other source connectors retain ownership of geography, query and trip data.

title: Add direct mouse interaction and drag placement to Canvas
description: Build the renderer-neutral Canvas interaction engine needed for immediate direct manipulation: hit testing, pointer capture, click-to-focus, drag-to-move, resize handles, z-order promotion, and predictable edge/grid snapping. The iced shell will translate native mouse events into this engine and apply validated workspace patches so agents and humans share the same placement model.
design: Keep input normalization and interaction state in dock-canvas library. Renderers supply logical pointer events and current surface geometry. The engine returns deterministic intents; the authoritative workspace/runtime validates and applies them. No OS mouse injection or Accessibility permission belongs here.
acceptance_criteria: Focused tests cover hit order, click focus, captured drags outside original bounds, move and resize constraints, release/cancel, and deterministic snapping; interaction state emits typed intents/patches without owning renderer or OS state; integration points are documented for iced, touch, and later XR pointers.
notes:
Implemented renderer-neutral direct manipulation in crates/dock-canvas/src/interaction.rs with normalized logical pointer events, ordered z-aware hit testing, eight resize handles, focus/front promotion, pointer capture, move/resize bounds intents, release/cancel restoration, workspace/minimum-size constraints, and stable edge-before-grid snap tie-breaking. Module docs define iced, touch, and XR adapter boundaries. Focused validation passed in isolated CARGO_TARGET_DIR=/Volumes/DOC MOVIES/dock-agent-interaction: 6 interaction tests and cargo clippy -p dock-canvas --lib -- -D warnings.
Live macOS proof completed: converted the running two-surface workspace to Canvas layout and injected a real pointer drag over mmd-diagram. Bounds moved from x=0.70,y=0.48 to x=0.6375,y=0.41148937; focus changed to mmd-diagram; z layer promoted from 1 to 3; authoritative document revision advanced. Runtime remained live on the right display.
close_reason: Interaction engine and focused coverage complete; iced integration remains with the parent Canvas shell work.

title: canvas_screenshot: render offscreen instead of shelling out to screencapture
notes:
canvas_screenshot shells out to the macOS `screencapture` binary (mcp.rs:1099) and then checks that
the surface's chrome appears in the captured pixels (mcp.rs:1081). So an agent cannot see the wall
whenever Canvas is occluded, on another Space, or the caller is a macOS Background session - all of
which happened repeatedly on 2026-09-10, and the failure mode is that an agent acts on the wall
blind while believing it looked.

VERDICT: A TRUE OFFSCREEN RENDER IS FEASIBLE TODAY AND THE API ALREADY EXISTS.
`iced::window::screenshot(id) -> Task<Screenshot>` (iced_runtime-0.14.0/src/window.rs:480-485,
re-exported at iced-0.14.0/src/window.rs:7-8) renders the widget tree into a PRIVATE OFFSCREEN
TEXTURE and reads it back as RGBA. Returns `Screenshot { rgba: Bytes, size, scale_factor }`
(iced_core-0.14.0/src/window/screenshot.rs:9-18) with a `crop()`; Bytes is Send+Sync+Clone so it is
safe in a Message.

WHY OCCLUSION CANNOT AFFECT IT, verified rather than assumed:
- iced_wgpu-0.14.0/src/lib.rs:180-296 creates its own texture `iced_wgpu.offscreen.source_texture`,
  draws into it, copies to a buffer and un-pads. NO wgpu::Surface appears in that function.
- The trait signatures say it structurally: iced_graphics-0.14.0/src/compositor.rs - `present` takes
  `surface: &mut Self::Surface` (:80-87), `screenshot` takes only `renderer` (:89-98).
- iced_winit-0.14.0/src/lib.rs:1637-1653 handles the action against the window's RENDERER and never
  queries visibility or occlusion.
- The retained layer stack stays fresh: interface.draw runs every RedrawRequested before present
  (iced_winit lib.rs:950-957, :981) and layers are only cleared by the next draw's reset. On macOS
  winit's redraw pump is not visibility-gated (winit-0.30.13 macos/app_state.rs:384-390), and Canvas
  subscribes to a >=30 Hz tick (main.rs:7115-7121), so the retained frame is never more than ~33 ms
  stale.

PRECEDENT IN THIS WORKSPACE: crates/canvas-mac/src/main.rs:483-486 and resource_palette.rs:302-321
already use iced::window::screenshot behind DOCK_SCREENSHOT. Caveat: canvas-mac is tiny-skia
(Cargo.toml:9), not wgpu - so that proves the API shape compiles here, not the wgpu path.

THE REPLY MUST BE A PATH, NOT BYTES, and this is not a preference. MAX_CONTROL_MESSAGE is 256 KB
(control.rs:20, enforced at control.rs:1089, :1137, main.rs:6989, :7023). A 5760x1200 RGBA readback
is 27.6 MB before encoding. Both processes are on one machine behind an owner-local 0600 socket and
mcp.rs:1088-1096 already round-trips through temp_dir, so a path plus a sha256 receipt is the same
trust boundary and no new one. It also converges with dock-qwv: a sha256-keyed capture is a
data-plane artifact in exactly the sense that bead describes, and media.rs:47-72's
MediaCacheKey::stable_string is the existing key format.

WHAT IT DELETES, which is a real part of the case: verify_surface_chrome (mcp.rs:1032-1086, ~55
lines), capture_region (mcp.rs:1088-1134, ~47 lines), and the whole double-inspect race guard
(mcp.rs:872-919) - because Canvas answers the capture atomically at a known revision inside one
execute, so the view cannot change between check and readback. CaptureChromeSnapshot
(control.rs:755-761) becomes dead weight. The Linux `grim` path goes too.

COST: ~250-400 lines net across a protocol boundary, plus tests. Not small, which is why it was
designed rather than implemented. Three of the match sites are exhaustive with no wildcard, so the
compiler finds omissions - but each discovery costs a full 8-40 minute cycle on a 9,669-line
main.rs.
PHASE 1, GENUINELY SMALL (~120 lines): restrict to the single-window case - resolve the region,
require it to fall inside exactly one window's Rect, and fail loudly otherwise. Covers the common
case, since a surface normally sits on one display. Phase 2 adds multi-window stitching.

FALLBACK REJECTED, having been costed: `screencapture -l <CGWindowID>` captures a window's own
contents, but on macOS winit's WindowId is a POINTER, not a window number
(winit-0.30.13 macos/window.rs:123-124). Getting a real CGWindowID means raw_window_handle -> NSView
-> [[view window] windowNumber] via objc2-app-kit: comparable effort to the real fix, still needs
Screen Recording permission, still fails from a Background session.

CAVEATS TO DESIGN AGAINST:
- device.poll(Wait) (iced_wgpu lib.rs:283-286) is a SYNCHRONOUS GPU STALL ON THE UI THREAD, so a
  full-wall capture will visibly hitch the wall. Not measured.
- Task::batch(...).collect() ends when the stream ends, so a window closed mid-capture yields a
  SHORT Vec rather than an error. The handler must check the length or it silently returns a partial
  wall - which is the fabrication rule again: an incomplete picture presented as the whole.
- If one-frame freshness needs to be airtight rather than argued, issue the screenshot from the
  RedrawRequested arm (main.rs:7122-7126), which iced broadcasts after the draw.

NOTHING WAS COMPILED. No claim here is that it builds.

title: [epic] Power On: the first five minutes as the real path, not a scripted demo
notes:
THE DEMO, AS AVERY DESCRIBES IT (2026-09-10). Not a pitch deck - the product's first five minutes,
built as the real path so that keeping the demo working is the same work as keeping the product
working.

POWER ON
  `fpl login` -> SSO -> downloads binary fast -> boots
  FPL spinning logo with SFX; Canvas workspace opens with a horizontal centre line opening out like
  an old TV
  JARVIS boot animation; establishes presence and identity
  "Good afternoon, Avery. What would you like to work on today?" -> most recent project / home

INTRO BRIEFING
  For newcomers: a briefing explaining JARVIS / Alfalfa / Canvas, then "what would you like to work
  on?"
  SPEC -> BUILD -> DEPLOY, in real time. Two hours. Then plans.
  Fully buildable on FPL cloud.
  Billing: flat fee plus cloud costs, possibly more nuanced.
  Invite to shared projects - CawLaw (dad + Ben), Ohm (the Jameses), Player (John) - with
  get-up-to-speed briefings per project, automatically updated.

WHY THIS IS NOT THROWAWAY, and the single constraint that decides it: THE DEMO MUST RUN THE REAL
PATH. The moment there is a --demo flag taking a different code route it rots within a month and
lies before that. The mechanism already exists and is already built: Provenance::Demo marks DATA as
synthetic while the CODE PATH stays identical. Same rule as "the disk-backed store must satisfy the
contract, not the demo". A generated briefing (dock-ybc.2) is a feature that happens to be
demoable; a scripted one is a liability.

FOUR THINGS TO DESIGN AGAINST NOW:

1. POLISH AND SUBSTANCE FAIL IN OPPOSITE DIRECTIONS, AND POLISH IS THE DANGEROUS ONE. A logo with
   SFX and a TV-open sets an expectation; if what follows takes 40 seconds to show a project, the
   intro makes it WORSE - promised Iron Man, delivered a loading screen. Measure cold `fpl login` to
   first useful screen BEFORE dressing it, and spend the animation budget covering real latency
   rather than adding to it. dock-ybc.4 (demo-mode latency budget, probe the machine, degrade by
   LoD) comes first, not after.

2. "GOOD AFTERNOON, AVERY" IS AN IDENTITY CLAIM AND IT IS THE FIRST THING ON SCREEN.
   PresenceSignalState already distinguishes Unavailable / Unknown / Detected / Verified. Greeting
   BY NAME must require Verified and degrade to a nameless greeting otherwise. A system that
   confidently calls someone the wrong name once is never trusted again, and this is the most
   visible possible place for it to happen.

3. BILLING IS CATEGORICALLY DIFFERENT from everything else on the list - regulated, adversarial,
   hard to reverse. "Flat fee plus cloud costs" requires PER-PROJECT COST ATTRIBUTION before
   anything can be billed, and metering cannot be applied retroactively. Either it is designed for
   real or it is explicitly out of the demo. It must not ride in as a checkbox.

4. THE INVITE FLOW IS WHERE THE SECURITY MODEL GETS ITS FIRST REAL TEST. Those are actual external
   people, so dock-ybc.11's assemble-per-scope and fail-closed-on-unresolved-identity become
   load-bearing on day one. Good, because it forces the right thing early - and it means the invite
   path cannot be demo-grade.

CONNECTS TO WORK ALREADY DONE: the agent roster (working_set + roster mapping) is what makes the
spec-build-deploy segment watchable rather than a progress bar - "see the swarm working" is the
difference between two hours of demo and two hours of waiting.
CORRECTIONS (Avery, same day):
- BILLING IS NOT PART OF THIS. It was swept in from an adjacent list and is planned in its own docs.
  Point 3 above should be read as "billing is out of scope here", not as a design note for this
  epic. Nothing in Power On should assume a billing surface exists.
- SEQUENCING: dock-ybc.12.1 (key hierarchy) IS needed, but the demo comes before inviting anyone, so
  it is NOT a near-term priority. Shared-project invites are downstream of a working demo, which
  means the per-scope key wrapping is downstream too. Do not pull it forward on account of point 4.
- NEXT: dock-ybc.4, the latency budget. It gates the polish rather than following it.

title: Canvas as artifact broker: four MCP tools, retrieval IS the attention signal
notes:
DESIGN (Avery, 2026-09-10). Canvas is a BROKER, not a data layer. The agent-visibility milestone -
"see the stuff the agent pulls" - is reached by making retrieval itself the signal, over the
smallest MCP surface that can carry it.

THE INSIGHT THAT MAKES IT BETTER THAN AN ATTENTION CONTRACT: attention becomes a SIDE EFFECT OF
RETRIEVAL. If every read goes through get_artifact, Canvas sees what the agent pulled BY
CONSTRUCTION - there is no second channel to emit on, no discipline to forget, and no way for
declared attention to drift from what was actually read. This dissolves dock-8cd's emit-versus-
imperative problem rather than solving it, and it IS dock-336 ("route retrieval through MCP so
Canvas sees it first"). It also retires canvas_open_file as the mechanism: the agent never places
anything, so nine agents cannot strobe the wall.

THE SURFACE - FOUR TOOLS:
  get_artifact     - research-wing, project files, wiki. Pure read. The retrieval that is also the
                     attention signal.
  save_artifact    - writes to project files. research-wing is public provenance; wiki is
                     generated/imported. A save may trigger a wiki update, deferred to show up in
                     search.
  search_artifacts - RAG over wiki / research / projects. The query AND its hits are themselves worth
                     showing; a result set is an artifact, which keeps the surface uniform.
  crop_artifact    - the "zoom", over image or PDF.
Kept separate from get_artifact because one is pure and one materialises; mixing a read and a
derivation in one tool is hard to reason about later. It is deterministic, so it is a derivation
with a cache rather than a write.

NO switch_project. Scope is keyed in the artifact call. A mode is state the agent must track, and
losing track of it is the failure already on record in dock-8cd - an agent applied a background to a
project nobody was looking at and reported success. It is also the "filter afterwards" pattern
dock-ybc.11 rules out; a scoped id in the call is "assemble per scope".

TWO IDS, ONE OBJECT, AND THEY DO DIFFERENT JOBS. A sha256 tells you the CONTENT, not the project -
two projects holding the same PDF hash identically, which is exactly right for dedupe and exactly
wrong for identity. So: a bead-style LOGICAL ID carries scope and provenance and is what callers
name; the CONTENT HASH is the storage key and is what dedupes underneath. This is the git model,
blobs content-addressed and trees giving them names. Do not collapse them into one string.

CROP REMOVES WORK RATHER THAN ADDING IT. If a crop PRODUCES AN ARTIFACT rather than parameterising a
view, region-level attention needs no new surface kind at all - no MediaVariant::PdfRegion, no rect
plumbed through MediaPlan. A crop is an artifact with a parent and a rect in its lineage. That was
listed as missing work on dock-8cd; this design deletes it.

TWO CHANNELS, NOT ONE - AND THE REASON IS A CORRECTNESS ONE. Artifacts cannot cover everything. An
agent that reads a file with `cat`, or fetches a URL directly, leaves no artifact - and the wall
would then look COMPLETE WHILE BEING PARTIAL. That is docs/widget-quality.md rule 1 at the system
level: a coherent picture that silently omits things is worse than an obviously incomplete one. So:
  ARTIFACTS - documents, images, PDFs, crops, result sets, saved outputs. Canvas SHOWS them.
  DIGEST    - what the agent is working on, files touched, shell commands and exit codes, blocked or
              not. Small, slowly-changing, computed ON THE AGENT HOST. Canvas SUMMARISES it.
The sorting test is "would you want to open it?".

THEREFORE DO NOT INSTRUCT AGENTS TO SAVE THEIR THINKING AS ARTIFACTS. Instructions are the weakest
available mechanism and it is the same discipline problem this design exists to avoid. Reasoning is
already in the transcript, and dock-zqe already concluded the right surface there is the digest, not
the text. Shell is the same shape: `cargo test` output is ephemeral, "ran cargo test, exit 1" is the
signal. Computing the digest on the agent host also keeps the firehose off the network, which is
dock-qwv's control-plane/data-plane split applied here.

CODE EDITS ARE THE ONE THING THAT CANNOT BE AN ARTIFACT - a checkout is mutable and large - so
stream deltas. Build the stream and the widget first and defer the agent wiring, which is now
cheaper than it was: StreamInbox retains rather than drains, so a screen joining late can catch up
instead of rendering a diff with no base.
CORRECTION TO THE "TWO IDS" NOTE ABOVE (Avery, 2026-09-10). One id - the sha256 - plus a BACKLINK
INDEX IN ALFALFA. Not a logical id alongside a content hash.

WHY THE EARLIER NOTE WAS WRONG. It reached for the git model, but git has trees because git needs
PATHS. This needs MEMBERSHIP, and membership is a relation, not a name. Introducing a second
addressing id creates the exact drift it was meant to prevent: two names for one blob, or a name
whose content moved underneath it. A content address plus a relation has no such surface.

AND SHARING FALLS OUT rather than being special-cased. An artifact belonging to two projects is
simply two backlinks. Under a scoped-id scheme it would have to be copied or aliased, and then the
copies drift.

ALFALFA OWNS IT, not Canvas. Alfalfa already owns project and resource identity, so the backlink
index belongs there and Canvas stays a broker (tenet 10). Canvas asks; it does not keep its own map.

TWO CONSEQUENCES THAT NOW HAVE TO BE DESIGNED FOR:

1. AUTHORISATION CANNOT BE IMPLIED BY THE ID. A content-derived address is guessable-by-possession -
   anyone who has seen the hash, including in a transcript or a log line, holds the address. So
   get_artifact(hash) must authorise against the backlink index and the CALLER'S SCOPE on every
   read, and must never treat possession of the hash as permission. This is stricter than a scoped
   id would have been, and better: it forces an explicit check instead of relying on names being
   unguessable. It is also dock-ybc.11's rule - assemble per scope at the point of use - landing
   exactly where it should.

2. DELETING STOPS MEANING DELETING. With dedupe and shared backlinks, a project removing an artifact
   drops a backlink while the blob survives for the other referrers. Correct, but it makes "I
   removed that from my project" and "that is gone" different statements, and for anything sensitive
   that difference is the whole thing. Decide NOW whether there is a purge that outranks the index -
   retrofitting one onto a content-addressed store is painful, and the sensitive case is exactly
   when someone will ask for it.

BONUS: THE BACKLINK INDEX IS THE PROVENANCE RECORD. It already has to know which projects claim an
artifact, when, and whether it arrived imported or generated - which answers the research-wing
(public provenance) versus wiki (generated/imported) distinction with no second mechanism, and gives
get_artifact something true to say about where a thing came from.
CAPABILITY SPLIT (Avery, 2026-09-10): "granular switching/control should exist, but only for the
specialized JARVIS agent or my active agent... So I can see the swarm working, but they can't hijack
my screens by accident."

BUILT, in crates/canvas/src/mcp.rs:
- `Role { Broker, Control }`. Broker is the four artifact tools. Control is those plus the existing
  nineteen, including every tool that can move a screen.
- ENFORCED BY OMISSION, not refusal. `list_tools`/`get_tool` return `tools_for(self.role)`, so a
  swarm agent never sees canvas_open_file at all. A tool an agent can see is a tool it will try, and
  a refusal it has to handle is worse than a capability it never knew about. `call_tool` ALSO checks
  by name, because a name can be guessed from documentation.
- `Canvas::default()` is Control and `Canvas::broker()` is the opt-DOWN. That direction is
  deliberate: the existing transports are already the human's own - stdio reaches only a process its
  caller spawned, and the loopback port sits behind a bearer only the bridge holds - so defaulting
  to Broker would have silently broken them. A swarm connection is a new thing and must ask.
- Tests assert the swarm surface is EXACTLY four tools, that none of the nine placement tools appear
  in it, that Control is a superset, and that no name is advertised twice.

STILL TO DO on the transport: nothing today constructs `Canvas::broker()`. The role exists and is
enforced; deciding how a connection earns Control - a second bearer, a separate port, or an
identity from fpl-auth - is the remaining piece, and it should reuse dock-ybc.20's agent-scoped
principals rather than invent a second notion of who is calling.

THE FOUR TOOLS ARE DEFINED BUT NOT SERVED. Schemas, descriptions and validation are in place;
calling one returns an explicit "not yet served: no artifact broker is connected" naming what is
missing, rather than an empty result that would read as "no artifacts". The fan-out to project
files, research-wing and the wiki is the next piece of work and needs Alfalfa's backlink index.
THE INDEX / CONTENT SPLIT (Avery, 2026-09-10): "alfalfa is gonna be running locally. that is the
manifest/index of all the artefacts. Probably of all the streams too. Per project. So plan for that
split. You may need to fan-out to actually retrieve context. That is TBD."

SO get_artifact IS TWO OPERATIONS, NOT ONE, and keeping them distinct is the whole design:
  1. RESOLVE, against local Alfalfa. Does this hash exist; is it backlinked to this project; may this
     caller read it; which store holds it; what type is it; where did it come from.
  2. FETCH, from wherever step 1 says. Fan-out. TBD.

WHY THE SPLIT IS LOAD-BEARING RATHER THAN INCIDENTAL:
- AUTHORIZATION HAPPENS IN STEP 1, against the index, never against the hash. This is where the
  earlier decision lands in code: possession of a content address is not permission, because a hash
  leaks in transcripts and log lines.
- THE TWO FAILURES MEAN DIFFERENT THINGS AND MUST NOT COLLAPSE INTO ONE ERROR. "No such artifact, or
  not yours" is a real and final answer. "The store holding it is unreachable" is a temporary
  condition. Reporting the second as the first tells an agent something false about the world, and
  it is the same distinction docs/widget-quality.md rule 3 draws between no data and cannot reach
  the source.
- CONTENT ADDRESSING MAKES STEP 2 CACHEABLE FOREVER. Bytes fetched for a hash never need
  revalidating, so Canvas can cache aggressively with no coherence protocol. media.rs ALREADY keys
  its cache by sha256 (MediaCacheKey) and main.rs already keeps background_assets in a sha256 map -
  the cache Canvas needs is the shape it already has.

CANVAS KEEPS NO INDEX OF ITS OWN. Alfalfa owns project and resource identity (tenet 10); anything
Canvas holds is a cache whose source of truth is elsewhere and which must be invalidatable. The
moment Canvas starts answering "which artifacts does this project have" from its own state, it has
become the data layer it was explicitly not supposed to be.

STREAMS IN THE INDEX TOO, and that reaches further than it looks. If Alfalfa lists a project's
streams, then the stream registry stops being Canvas configuration and becomes something discovered
per project - which is the same move dock-qwv.1 makes for views. A screen would then learn what a
project HAS (control plane) separately from subscribing to it (data plane), which is exactly
dock-qwv's split arriving from the index side rather than the transport side.

WHAT IS STILL OPEN: the fan-out itself - whether Canvas calls the stores directly, or the bridge
brokers it the way metric_reads does for Prometheus. The bridge pattern is the better default on
precedent: named operations, host attaches credentials, bounded returns, no arbitrary-path
passthrough. Decide when the index lands.
WHAT CANVAS NEEDS FROM THE ALFALFA MANIFEST (Avery asked: should Alfalfa define it? Just REST? What
about save_artifact updating the index?)

ALFALFA DEFINES IT. It owns identity, so it owns the schema; Canvas designing it would make the
broker the data layer's architect, which is what "we are not the data layer" rules out. But an
interface designed without knowing its consumer is worse than one designed with it, so this is what
Canvas needs in a manifest ENTRY in order to render honestly. Every field below is here because a
widget lies without it:

  id           sha256. Identity, and the fetch key.
  name         what a human searches and reads. Without it the palette lists hashes.
  fmt          content type. Needed twice: to pick a renderer, and for `fmt:img` filtering.
  bytes        size. Needed to decide whether to fetch before showing, and to warn before a
               200 MB pull onto a wall.
  store        project | research | wiki. PROVENANCE. Without it a generated wiki page and a
               first-party project file render identically, which is the fabrication rule.
  projects     the backlinks. Scope, sharing, and the authorization check.
  created_at   when the content came into being.
  indexed_at   when SEARCH last saw it - nullable, and the nullability is the point. See below.

REST IS THE RIGHT DEFAULT for query: boring, cacheable, read-mostly (tenet 11). But polling is the
wrong way to keep a palette current, so pair it with a CHANGE FEED, and reuse the shape we already
have rather than inventing a second one: the index publishes changes onto a stream carrying a
SEQUENCE, and Canvas follows it exactly as it follows widget snapshots. That gives the palette
freshness without polling AND lets a client that fell behind know it missed something, which polling
never can.

SAVE_ARTIFACT AND THE INDEX - the split that matters:
- THE BACKLINK IS SYNCHRONOUS. save_artifact must not return until the artifact is retrievable and
  authorized, or an agent cannot read back what it just wrote, which is an infuriating and
  hard-to-diagnose class of bug.
- SEARCH INDEXING MAY LAG, and the manifest must SAY SO. That is what `indexed_at: null` is for. A
  search that misses a just-saved artifact is then explainable - "saved, not yet indexed" - instead
  of looking exactly like "that artifact does not exist". Avery already called this: "save could
  cause a wiki update to happen - which is real, but that might be deferred to end up in search."
  Deferral is fine; SILENT deferral is not (tenet 12).
- So a palette showing a just-saved artifact should be able to show it as pending rather than
  omitting it.

ONE THING TO PUSH BACK ON IF IT COMES UP: do not let the manifest return content inline, even for
small artifacts. Resolve and fetch are separate for a reason (see the notes above) - collapsing them
makes "not found" and "store unreachable" the same failure again.
CORRECTION: the claim above that crop-as-artifact deletes the need for region rendering holds only for the STATIC case. Animating a zoom needs parent-at-rect rendered client side, so the region capability is required after all - as a view transform, not an index entry. See the animated-crop bead: crop is a POINTER by default and only becomes an artifact on explicit promotion, or a sixty-frame zoom would mint sixty hashes.

title: Saved views live in a store: externally sourced, remotely saved, validated at load
notes:
DIRECTION (Avery, 2026-09-10): SAVED VIEWS MUST BE EXTERNALLY SOURCED AND SAVED REMOTELY. They stop
being compiled-in artifacts and become documents in a store.

WHERE THEY ARE TODAY, verified: operational_views.rs:35-37 resolves a view name to an `include_str!`
of config/views/*.json. They are compiled into the binary. Nothing mutates a view's sources at
runtime - a grep for assignment to `.position` in that file returns nothing - and there is no save
path at all.

WHAT THIS RESOLVES. It revives the step that could not be done: `SourcePosition::Live {
observed_sequence }` is meaningless in a compiled constant, because a constant cannot record
anything. A stored view CAN record where it was, which is what makes a screen resumable and what
makes a share link a position rather than "whatever arrives after it opens".

IT ALSO ANSWERS PART OF dock-qwv's ONE-WAY DOOR. If views live in a store, the backend is
authoritative for view documents, not only for content. Combined with the log-authoritative
recommendation, the division becomes: the store owns VIEWS (what should be shown) and the log owns
EVENTS (what happened), and a screen projects a rendering from both. reconcile.rs still reconciles a
local document; that document is now derived from two remote inputs rather than one local file.

THE REGRESSION TO DESIGN AGAINST, and it is not obvious. `include_str!` means a malformed view is a
COMPILE ERROR today, and operational_views.rs:614 asserts exactly that -
`every_named_view_is_a_valid_shared_view_document`. A remotely sourced view cannot have that
guarantee. Validation has to move to load time and fail LOUDLY (tenet 12) - a view that will not
parse must say so on the screen, not render as an empty wall that looks like a quiet system. Keep
the build-time test for the views we ship; add a load-time one for the views we fetch.

CONSEQUENCES TO CARRY:
- A screen with no route to the store must still show its last known view, MARKED STALE. Same rule
  as consequence 3 above; now it applies to the view itself and not only to its data.
- Views become mutable and shared, so an edit on one screen has to reach another. That is the same
  sequencing problem as the event log, and it should reuse it rather than invent a second one.
- Views become user data. Scope, OIDC and the assemble-per-scope rule (dock-ybc.11) apply to them -
  a view is exactly the kind of thing that leaks by being fetched with the wrong principal.
- dock-8nz (share a view as a link) stops needing a serialisation format of its own: a link becomes
  a reference into the store plus a position.
CORRECTION TO THIS BEAD'S PREMISE, and it splits the work into three parts of which one was already
done. I claimed views are compiled-in constants. Half wrong.

1. EXTERNALLY SOURCED - ALREADY TRUE, and it was true before this bead was filed.
   operational_views::load (operational_views.rs:20) tries crate::runtime_config::read on
   `views/<name>.json` FIRST, parses it, calls document.validate(), checks that the id matches the
   name, and only falls through to the include_str! copy when no such file exists.
   runtime_config::root() is $CANVAS_CONFIG_DIR, else ~/Library/Application Support/Dock/canvas on
   macOS, else $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/dock/canvas. So the built-in views are a FALLBACK, and load-time
   validation already exists and already fails loudly. The regression I warned about in the note
   above does not apply: it was designed for correctly from the start.

2. SAVED - WAS MISSING, NOW ADDED. runtime_config had `read` and nothing else, so a view could be
   authored by hand but never written by Canvas. That is the reason SourcePosition::Live {
   observed_sequence } could not be recorded - not that views were constants, but that nothing could
   write one back.
   Added runtime_config::write (atomic: temp file plus rename, so a crash mid-write leaves the
   previous document intact rather than a truncated one that load() would then correctly refuse) and
   operational_views::save, which validates and checks the id BEFORE writing - a document that would
   not load must not reach the disk. One MAX_VIEW_BYTES ceiling now serves both directions, so a
   document that saves is a document that loads back.

3. REMOTE - STILL MISSING, and it is now the only part left. root() is a local directory. The shape
   to aim for is a store trait with the local-filesystem implementation as one impl and the
   backend-served one as another, so the remote version is a second implementation rather than a
   rewrite. Everything that has to be true of a remote store - validate on load, fail loud, atomic
   replace, revision-carrying documents - is now exercised locally by tests.

WORTH KNOWING FOR THE SEQUENCING: SharedViewDocument already carries `revision: u64`
(view.rs:172). The versioning hook a multi-writer store needs is already in the document format;
nothing bumps it yet.

title: Mint agent-scoped sessions from fpl-auth rather than injecting the human's cookies
notes:
INJECT AN AGENT-SCOPED SESSION, NEVER A COPY OF THE HUMAN'S. Avery's opening is right - we can inject
cookies for SSO from fpl login / enrollment - and the thing to get right on day one is WHOSE session
it is.

Owning the IdP is what makes this better than any browser isolation story. Playwright --isolated
(dock-ybc.16) gives an agent a clean cookie jar; it does not give it a DIFFERENT IDENTITY. Because we
own fpl-auth, `fpl login` / enrollment can MINT A SESSION WHOSE PRIVILEGES ARE THE AGENT'S. That is
strictly stronger: the blast radius of a prompt-injected agent is bounded by what that principal can
do, not by what the human can do.

CONTRAST WITH THE FAILURE MODE ALREADY MEASURED (dock-ybc.16): claude-in-chrome's MCP tab group lives
in the human's Brave Default profile, so an agent navigating anywhere the human is logged in arrives
authenticated AS THEM. That is the thing we are deliberately not rebuilding. Copying a cookie is the
same mistake with extra steps.

REQUIREMENTS:
- The injected session is an agent principal with its own OIDC scopes, per dock-ybc.11's rule that
  scope is assembled at the point of use rather than filtered afterwards.
- Short TTL, and revocable independently of the human's session. Killing an agent's access must not
  log the human out, and logging the human out must not silently leave an agent authenticated.
- The agent never receives the cookie value. Same invariant as the bridge's egress pattern: the host
  attaches it, the caller names an operation. An agent that can read its own session cookie can
  exfiltrate it.
- Audit: which agent, which principal, which origin, when. Same trail as the credential broker
  (dock-ybc.12), and subject to the same metadata question (dock-ybc.12.2) - the audit log is itself
  a leak of the same shape.

THIS ALSO REPLACES THE COOKIE-INJECTION SHORTCUT LATER. Once dock-ybc.12.4 gives us our own
authenticator, an agent-scoped session can be established by a real assertion against our own IdP
rather than by injecting state. Cookie injection is the bootstrap, not the destination - write it so
it can be removed.

title: Decide the metadata encryption boundary field by field - this is what sank LastPass
notes:
THE OTHER ONE-WAY DOOR, and the one that actually sinks password managers. LastPass's 2022 breach was
catastrophic not because the cipher broke but because the vaults' URLs WERE NOT ENCRYPTED - so an
attacker with the stolen blobs learned exactly who banked where, and could phish precisely while
brute-forcing at leisure. The cipher was fine. The metadata boundary was the vulnerability.

DECIDE EXPLICITLY, field by field, what the server can see:
- Item name, URL/origin, username, folder, tags, TOTP seed, notes, attachment names, item COUNT,
  item SIZES, access timestamps.
Each one is either encrypted or it is a capability the server needs - searching, sharing checks,
origin matching for autofill. You cannot have both, so the interesting work is deciding which
capabilities are worth which leaks, and saying so.

NOTE THE TENSION WITH OUR OWN DESIGN: host-mediated filling needs ORIGIN MATCHING. If the host is a
vault client holding keys it can match on decrypted origins locally, and the server never needs
them. That is the right answer and it is only available because we chose the host-client
architecture - so this decision and the key hierarchy decision are coupled and should be made
together.

ALSO DECIDE WHAT WE LOG. An audit trail of "which agent asked for which credential at which origin"
is required by dock-ybc.12, and it is itself a metadata leak of the same shape. Encrypt or scope it
deliberately rather than discovering later that the audit log is the softest target in the system.

The deliverable is a table - field, encrypted y/n, what capability the exposure buys, what an
attacker with the database learns - published in the design doc, not implied by the schema.

title: Design the key hierarchy, sharing and recovery model before any secret is stored
notes:
TENET 4, THE GENUINE ONE-WAY DOOR. Every secret ever stored is encrypted under whatever hierarchy we
pick on day one. Changing it later means a migration that decrypts and re-encrypts every item for
every user - the one operation this system exists to make impossible to do carelessly. Get it right
before any real credential goes in.

WHAT HAS TO BE DECIDED, not implemented, before code:
- Master key derivation. Argon2id parameters, and where they are stored so they can be RAISED later
  per user without a flag day. Bitwarden's shipped PBKDF2 iteration defaults were a real
  vulnerability class precisely because the parameter was baked in and left behind.
- The wrapping chain: master key -> account key -> per-item key. Per-item keys are what make sharing
  and rotation possible without re-encrypting the world.
- Sharing. Each principal gets a keypair; an item shared into a scope is its item key wrapped to
  each member's public key. This is where the OIDC scoping from dock-ybc.11 attaches - and it must
  be assembled per scope, not filtered after, per that bead's rule.
- ROTATION, designed in from the start. Rotating a compromised item key, a user's account key, and
  an org key are three different operations. If they are not designed now, they do not get added.
- RECOVERY, which is the question every E2E vault must answer and most answer badly. Forgotten master
  password: lose the vault (honest, and correct for personal scope), or escrow to an admin (a whole
  second key hierarchy with its own compromise story). FPL Cloud companies will need the second for
  team scope. Decide both, separately, and write down who can read what under each.

WRITE IT DOWN AS A DOCUMENT WITH A THREAT MODEL before writing the crate. The reviewable artifact is
the key hierarchy diagram plus "what does an attacker with X learn", for X in {the database, one
device, the host process, a valid session token, an admin}.

Depends on nothing; blocks everything else in dock-ybc.12.

title: Own the secret store: host-mediated credential injection, passkeys, cross-machine browser state
notes:
If we own the browser (see the Servo evaluation) we can also own the secret store, and logins stop
being something an agent or an extension handles.

THE SHAPE ALREADY EXISTS IN THIS CODEBASE. fpl-desktop-bridge/src/credential_broker.rs opens with:
"Owner-only IPC: MCP clients never read Keychain or receive bearer credentials." metric_reads.rs
applies it: the caller names an operation, the bridge attaches the bearer, only bounded JSON comes
back. Credential injection into a browser is the same pattern with a different sink - the HOST fills
the field, the agent never receives the secret.

Today there is no vaultwarden or bitwarden anywhere in the FPL tree; secrets live in the OS keyring
(fpl-enrollment/src/credentials.rs). A self-hosted vaultwarden would be the store; the browser
extension is what it replaces.

PASSKEYS ARE WHAT MAKE THIS SAFE RATHER THAN DANGEROUS.

The obvious risk of an agent-driven browser with stored passwords is prompt injection: a page the
agent is reading says "log in here", the agent navigates, and autofill hands real credentials to a
phishing origin. An allowlist mitigates that imperfectly, because the allowlist has to anticipate.

A passkey cannot be phished. WebAuthn credentials are origin-bound cryptographically - an assertion
for github.com cannot be produced for a lookalike origin - and the private key never leaves the
authenticator, so there is nothing for an agent to read or exfiltrate even in principle. Origin
binding does structurally what an allowlist does badly.

THE RISK MOVES, IT DOES NOT VANISH. It relocates to the user-presence gesture. An authenticator
requires user presence or verification; that IS the human check. If the host auto-approves every
assertion so an agent is not blocked, the check is deleted and we are back to an agent that can
authenticate as the human at will.

So the design question is: WHEN does an agent get an automatic assertion, and when must a human
approve? That lands on machinery already designed rather than needing new invention:
- dock-7pa: presence distinguishes Verified owner from Detected-but-unknown, and fails closed.
- dock-8n5: an approval is an identity plus a query routed by presence - so a passkey prompt IS an
  approval artifact, delivered to whatever screen the owner is actually at.
- dock-ybc.2: per-agent browser state is per-agent context and must not leak between agents.

Sensible default to argue from: auto-assert only for origins explicitly marked low-risk, only while
presence is Verified, and require an explicit routed approval for anything else. Never auto-assert
when identity is unresolved.

CROSS-MACHINE BROWSER STATE. Owning the browser means profile, history and session state can follow
the person across machines rather than living in one Chrome install. That is dock-qwv again - the
backend owns durable state and clients attach - so browser state is another store under the same
coordinator question rather than a new one. iOS is the known exception and is fine to exclude.

OPEN QUESTIONS, and the first is load-bearing:
- Does Servo support WebAuthn at all, and to what level? If it does not, passkeys in an owned browser
  are a research project rather than an integration, and the whole safety argument above is
  hypothetical. VERIFY THIS BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE.
- Where does the authenticator live? A software authenticator inside the coordinator is convenient
  and concentrates risk; a hardware key or the platform authenticator keeps the private key out of
  our process but is harder to reach from a headless instance on another machine.
- What is the audit trail? Every assertion should be recorded with which agent asked, for which
  origin, and whether a human approved. An agent authenticating as the owner without a durable record
  is not acceptable regardless of how safe the mechanism is.
TOTP AS WELL AS PASSKEYS. Vaultwarden stores TOTP seeds, so moving off Authy is a concrete win in its
own right (Authy's desktop app was discontinued and export is deliberately painful). The same
host-mediated shape applies: the host holds the seed, generates the code and fills it; the agent asks
to be logged in and never receives either.

BUT TOTP AND PASSKEYS ARE NOT EQUALLY SAFE HERE, and the difference decides the design.

A passkey is origin-bound cryptographically: an assertion for github.com cannot be produced for a
lookalike origin, so an agent tricked by prompt injection into visiting a phishing page simply gets
nothing. That is why passkeys make an agent-driven browser safe.

A TOTP CODE HAS NO ORIGIN BINDING. It is six digits that work anywhere they are typed. An agent
tricked into requesting a fill on a phishing origin hands over a valid code, and the phisher relays
it. TOTP restores exactly the attack passkeys remove.

Therefore, for TOTP specifically:
- The HOST must validate the origin before filling, because the credential cannot. This is the
  allowlist that passkeys do not need, and it has to be maintained.
- An agent must not be able to name an arbitrary origin for a fill. It requests a login for a known
  SERVICE; the host decides the origin.
- Prefer promoting a service to passkeys over automating its TOTP. Automating TOTP on a service that
  supports passkeys is choosing the phishable path.
- Anything high-value should require a routed human approval (dock-8n5) rather than an automatic
  fill, regardless of presence.

Audit applies identically: which agent asked, for which service and origin, whether a human approved.
LICENSING: THE STATED CONSTRAINT IS NOT MET. Verified against the GitHub API today, not recalled:
`dani-garcia/vaultwarden` is **AGPL-3.0** (`license.spdx_id`), and LICENSE.txt is the GNU Affero
General Public License v3 verbatim. Avery's condition was "just needs to not be AGPLv3", so this has
to be settled before a managed Vaultwarden per FPL Cloud company gets planned around.

AND THE PROBLEM IS CATEGORY-WIDE, not a Vaultwarden quirk. Bitwarden's own server is AGPL-3.0 and
Passbolt is AGPL-3.0. Self-hosted password managers pick AGPL precisely to stop someone reselling
them as SaaS - which is close to the shape of "a managed Vaultwarden per FPL Cloud company". So
"pick a different one" probably does not exist inside this category.

WHAT AGPL ACTUALLY REACHES, because the answer depends on which of these we do:
- Running it UNMODIFIED as an internal service: obligation is satisfied by pointing at upstream.
  Nothing of ours is touched.
- MODIFYING it and letting people use it over a network: AGPL s13 entitles THOSE NETWORK USERS to
  the Corresponding Source of our modified version. Internal staff are a small, known set; customers
  of an FPL Cloud company are not.
- Our own services talking to it over its HTTP API: separate programs, not derivative works. This is
  the normal reading and it is where the host-mediated filler would live.
- Linking Vaultwarden code into one of our binaries: derivative, copyleft attaches. Do not.
So the sharp edge is specifically (2) - offering a MODIFIED instance to customers. Staying on stock
Vaultwarden and putting all our behaviour in a separate service on the other side of its API keeps
us clear. That is also better architecture (tenet 2), which is a convenient alignment rather than a
coincidence.
NON-AGPL OPTION FOR THE SECRETS HALF ONLY: OpenBao (MPL-2.0, the fork made when Vault went BUSL). It
is not a password manager and has no Bitwarden client story, so it does not serve the browser-autofill
goal - but "move fpl-auth's secrets to it for storage" is exactly what it is for. Worth splitting the
two goals rather than making one tool carry both.

OIDC: YES, and this one is good news. SSO/OIDC is mainline Vaultwarden, not a fork - `sso_enabled`
appears in src/auth.rs, src/config.rs, src/api/{mod,web,admin}.rs and the admin templates on main
(1.37.2, released 2026-08-22). So the scoping model this epic already requires - OIDC-scoped, share
projects and agents, keep personal separate - lands on the vault too rather than needing a parallel
identity system. That is the Timshel SSO work, merged upstream; no third-party fork to track.

ARCHITECTURAL CONSTRAINT THAT SHAPES THE AI-FILLABLE 2FA DESIGN, and it is not obvious: in the
Bitwarden data model the TOTP seed lives INSIDE the end-to-end-encrypted cipher. The server never
sees it and cannot generate the code; the CLIENT generates it after decrypting with the user's key.
So "the host generates the code and fills it" means the host must be a real VAULT CLIENT holding a
key, not an API caller with a token. That is a materially bigger trust boundary than the bridge's
existing egress pattern, where the host attaches a bearer the caller never sees. Design it
deliberately: the host holding vault keys is the single most valuable target on the machine.
DIRECTION SET (Avery, 2026-09-10): BUILD IT. Apache-2.0, with easy export/import. Do not deploy
Vaultwarden as the answer; the AGPL finding above stops being a blocker and becomes the reason.

THE LICENCE PATH IS CLEAR - verified against crates.io and GitHub today, not recalled:
  passkey / passkey-authenticator  0.5.0   MIT OR Apache-2.0   1Password/passkey-rs, Apache-2.0,
                                                               pushed 2026-09-09, actively maintained
  webauthn-rs / -authenticator-rs  0.6.x   MPL-2.0             kanidm; file-level copyleft, so it
                                                               composes into an Apache-2.0 product
  totp-rs                          6.0.0   MIT
  argon2 (RustCrypto)              0.6.0   MIT OR Apache-2.0
  aws-lc-rs                        1.18.1  Apache-2.0 / ISC
Every primitive we need ships under a licence compatible with shipping ours as Apache-2.0. The
notable one: 1Password published the SOFTWARE AUTHENTICATOR half themselves, under Apache-2.0. The
hard cryptographic core of "be a passkey" is available; we are not writing CTAP from scratch.

THE MOAT IS NOT THE LICENCE, and the claim is stronger once stated correctly. Apache-2.0 plus real
export makes us ADOPTABLE WHERE AGPL BLOCKS ADOPTION - which is the actual reason to do it - but it
does not kill Bitwarden, whose moat is trust, published audits and client ubiquity. What incumbents
structurally cannot follow is the AGENT-NATIVE part: their whole architecture assumes a human clicks
approve. A broker where the credential is NON-EXTRACTABLE, the origin check is enforced by US, and
approval is routed rather than clicked is a category they would have to rearchitect to enter.

AND THAT IS WHAT MAKES AI-FILLABLE 2FA SAFE. If we are the authenticator, WE do the origin binding,
so a prompt-injected agent physically cannot obtain an assertion for a lookalike origin - the
credential refuses. Compare the TOTP note above: six digits work anywhere they are typed. So the
policy falls out of the architecture rather than being bolted on: prefer promoting a service to
passkeys over automating its TOTP, and treat TOTP automation as the phishable fallback that needs a
host-maintained origin allowlist.

ONE THING WE MUST NOT OVERCLAIM. If the host decrypts so agents never see plaintext, the end-to-end
property is between the user and THE HOST, not the user and the server. That is a weaker guarantee
than Bitwarden's and a more useful one for this use case. Say exactly that. Do not market it as
"zero-knowledge" - the same honesty rule as docs/widget-quality.md rule 1, applied to a security
claim instead of a chart.

SCOPE DISCIPLINE: the dangerous version of this project is "we build a password manager". The
defensible version is "we build a scoped secret broker for agents that happens to serve humans too".
Blast radius and client surface are the difference. iOS is conceded to the platform, as noted above.

title: Survey Prometheus and generate candidate dashboards per project
notes:
Survey a Prometheus job (or a group of targets) and emit CANDIDATE WIDGET DEFINITIONS - not a widget
per metric, and not a layout. A person or an LLM finishes it. This is what turns Canvas from a
sandbox into a dashboarding tool, because a new service becomes a dashboard in minutes rather than a
hand-written mapping.

TODAY: config/metrics.json is 21 hand-written sources, 11 of them backed. Every new service means
hand-authoring PromQL, picking widget kinds, and guessing units. That does not scale past a handful
of jobs, and it drifts the moment a service adds a metric.

BLOCKER, and it is small: fpl-desktop-bridge/src/metric_reads.rs allows only query, query_range and
/-/ready. The survey needs /api/v1/metadata, /api/v1/label/__name__/values and /api/v1/series. Those
are read-only and belong in the same allowlist, added the same way - no arbitrary path passthrough.

WHAT PROMETHEUS ALREADY TELLS US
- /api/v1/metadata gives TYPE (counter|gauge|histogram|summary), HELP and UNIT per metric. HELP is a
  free widget title.
- Name conventions carry semantics: _total (counter), _seconds, _bytes, _ratio, _info, _bucket.
- Label cardinality decides shape: one series, a small breakdown, or a matrix.
- `up` is special - a status list, not a number.

RULES, type + cardinality + unit -> widget kind
- counter, any cardinality      -> time_series of rate(...[5m]). A RAW COUNTER IS A MEANINGLESS RAMP;
                                   this single rule is most of what separates a useful generator from
                                   a naive one.
- gauge, 1 series               -> stat
- gauge, 2-12 series            -> ranked_bar for now, time_series over a window
- gauge, >12 series             -> heatmap, or top-N ranked_bar with the tail disclosed
- histogram (_bucket)           -> heatmap, or histogram_quantile for latency
- gauge in 0..1, or _ratio      -> gauge widget, scaled x100
- _info                         -> NOT a widget. It is label enrichment for other metrics.

FAMILY DETECTION - the part that makes it smart rather than mechanical
- X_used_bytes + X_bytes        -> ONE utilisation gauge, not two stats. config/metrics.json already
                                   hand-encodes exactly this for VRAM: 100 * used / total.
- X_total + X_errors_total      -> an error rate, not two counters
- _sum + _count                 -> an average
- longest common prefix         -> a panel group (bifrost_yggdrasil_accelerator_* is one family)

OUTPUT FORMAT: candidate widget definitions, NOT layout.
The shapes already exist - config/widgets/*.json for the widget spec and config/metrics.json for the
source mapping. The survey emits both, annotated with why each choice was made (type, cardinality,
family) so a reviewer can correct a wrong guess rather than re-deriving it. Layout stays derived:
dock-v7c size hints decide how much room each kind needs, and dock-blw display count decides how many
fit.

WHY THIS SPLIT IS THE RIGHT ONE: choosing a widget from metric metadata is deterministic and testable,
so it should be code. Deciding which six of forty candidates matter to a human is judgement, so it
should be a person or an LLM. Generating a layout is arithmetic over size hints, so it should be code
again. The LLM sits in the one place where taste is actually required.

HONESTY REQUIREMENTS
- A metric the heuristic cannot classify is REPORTED, not silently dropped or rendered as a stat.
  Silent omission is how a dashboard ends up quietly missing the metric that mattered.
- Every generated source states its provenance: which rule fired and on what evidence.
- Generated PromQL must be validated by executing it before being written, so a survey never emits a
  query that returns nothing. docs/widget-quality.md rule 3 applies to generated content too.

FIRST MOVE: add the three read-only metadata routes to metric_reads.rs, then a survey binary that
prints candidates for one job. No Canvas integration needed to prove the heuristic - the output is a
file a human can read and argue with.
close_reason: Closed

title: Context isolation: OIDC-scoped personal, team and project contexts with no leaks
notes:
Subconscious and Canvas both hold context that must not cross identity boundaries. Personal context, team context and per-project context are distinct, and sharing a project or an agent must not leak anything outside what was shared.

'No leaks in context' is the requirement, and it is a security property rather than a preference.

The principle already exists on the JARVIS side and must extend to Canvas. jarvis/distributed-topology.md: 'Conversation history is scoped to a resolved identity and session. Unknown speakers use a separate ephemeral session; a face observation alone must not silently give an unknown speaker another person's private history.'

That sentence is the whole design in miniature, and it generalises:
- Identity resolves a scope; it does not unlock a superset.
- Weaker evidence gets a NARROWER scope, never a shared one. An unknown speaker gets an ephemeral
  session, not the owner's history.
- Fail closed: unresolved identity means less context, not more.

What must be scoped:
- conversation history and session state (Subconscious)
- surfaces, views, workspaces and the artifact index (Canvas, dock-rk4)
- agent transcripts and attention (dock-8cd) - what an agent read is often the most revealing thing
- briefings and their read positions (dock-8n5), which differ per person even for one project

Design requirements:
- ASSEMBLE per scope rather than filter after. A briefing for a collaborator must be built from what
  they are entitled to see, not produced in full and then redacted. Filtering after assembly is how
  the wrong thing gets shown once, and once is enough.
- OIDC is the scope authority. fpl-auth already owns grants and scopes; neither service should grow
  a second permission model (tenet 10).
- Sharing is explicit and narrow: a shared project grants that project, not the sharer's other
  context. Sharing an agent grants that agent's outputs, not its whole transcript history.
- Personal remains personal by default. The default scope on anything unlabelled is the narrowest
  one, not the widest.
- dock-7pa (presence sensitivity) and dock-8nz (identity-gated links) are the RENDERING half of this;
  this bead is the STORAGE and ASSEMBLY half. They must agree on what a scope is.

title: Canvas backend and JARVIS Subconscious are one coordinator, not two
notes:
Read side by side, jarvis/distributed-topology.md (V1 contract for jarvis-8uz.10) and dock-qwv describe the same system:

  authoritative coordinator per installation   ~  backend owns cache and state
  sensor daemons register, publish snapshots   ~  screens attach and subscribe
  'a disconnected sensor cannot keep a room     ~  a screen cut off from its backend
   private indefinitely'                           admits staleness
  expired observations mean unknown context     ~  unknown presence fails closed,
   and RESERVED DISCLOSURE                          degrades rather than reveals

That last row is the striking one: two documents written by different sessions on different days independently arrived at fail-closed-on-stale-evidence.
