dedup'd and replicated, so the write path has to ask, and the default has to be the safe one for the
data class rather than whichever store is more convenient.

LIKELY CONTENTS: credentials in flight, TOTP seeds in transit (dock-ybc.12), agent transcripts that
captured a secret, anything under a customer retention limit.

ALSO RECORDED - IPFS AS A PULL-THROUGH EDGE CACHE rather than on every node. This removes most of
dock-ybc.23's objections: CNC controllers become clients rather than peers, so the heavy-daemon
problem goes away; the announce surface shrinks to a known tier; and it is the boring shape - a
registry mirror or CDN edge - rather than a novel one. Canvas already keeps a sha256-keyed cache, so
an edge node is that cache shared between the few machines worth sharing it between.
KEEP HONEST: a pull-through cache is still a copy. Sensitive data does not stop being a question, it
becomes a BOUNDED and AUDITABLE one - "which edge nodes hold what" is answerable where "every
machine in the lab" was not.

title: Artifact substrate: adopt the content-addressed shape now, defer IPFS until encrypt-then-address
notes:
IPFS AS THE ARTIFACT SUBSTRATE (Avery, 2026-09-10). Context: Canvas + JARVIS/presence is going on
most nodes anyway - lab, laptop, this machine, the CNC controllers - so an artifact store that is
already everywhere is attractive.

VERDICT: ADOPT THE SHAPE NOW, DEFER THE DAEMON. And there is one condition that flips the daemon
question, which is already on our roadmap.

WHY THE SHAPE IS RIGHT, and it is not a coincidence: we independently chose content addressing,
dedup underneath, and a separate mutable index. That IS IPFS's data model. Two things make it fit
behind the contract rather than through it:
- Alfalfa's resolve() returns OPAQUE LOCATORS and never fetches. A CID is a perfectly good locator,
  so IPFS would be an implementation detail of an interface that already exists.
- Canvas's cache is already sha256-keyed (MediaCacheKey, background_assets). A local IPFS node is
  approximately that cache, shared between nodes.
- Multi-node is the real topology. A single fpl-storage box makes it WORSE by round-tripping every
  artifact through one machine, and a CNC controller that loses the network still has what it
  pinned - which is dock-qwv consequence 3 satisfied by the storage layer rather than by Canvas.

WHY NOT KUBO YET:
1. PUBLIC BY INSTINCT. The DHT announces what you hold and Bitswap serves blocks to whoever asks.
   Against "no leaks in context, trusted private or team access" that is a real mismatch. A private
   swarm fixes it and is ALL-OR-NOTHING - one boundary, not per-project ones. That is exactly the
   sovereignty-boundary risk already raised: dedup ACROSS a boundary is the covert channel.
2. IPFS DOES NOT ENCRYPT. Either artifacts enter as ciphertext, or they sit in plaintext on every
   node that pins them. Plaintext on a lab CNC controller is not obviously acceptable.
3. DELETION GETS STRUCTURALLY WORSE. We already knew dropping a backlink does not drop bytes; IPFS
   distributes that, so unpinning locally says nothing about another node's pin. "Delete this"
   becomes close to unanswerable.
4. HEAVY NEIGHBOUR. Kubo is a large daemon with a chatty DHT and well-known disk and bandwidth
   surprises. Poor tenant on a machine driving a CNC. Tenet 11.

THE CONDITION THAT FLIPS IT - ENCRYPT-THEN-ADDRESS. If artifacts are encrypted with keys from the
vault work (dock-ybc.12), the CID is of CIPHERTEXT, THE BOUNDARY BECOMES THE KEY RATHER THAN THE
NETWORK, and deletion becomes key destruction rather than chasing pins. Objections 1-3 either
dissolve or become tractable; only operational weight survives. So the vault is what makes IPFS safe
here, and these two threads are not competing for attention - one unlocks the other.

NOTE THE ONE THING IPFS CANNOT DO FOR US EITHER WAY: mutable pointers. IPNS is slow and fragile, and
we need revisions and a current-revision concept. So the mutable layer stays in Alfalfa regardless,
which usefully sharpens the split: ALFALFA OWNS NAMES AND REVISIONS, THE BLOCK STORE ONLY EVER OWNS
BYTES.

TRIGGER TO REVISIT, measurable rather than aesthetic: when an artifact produced on one node is
wanted on another and the round-trip through a central store is actually hurting. Until then the
local-disk store teaches us the same contract at a fraction of the operational cost.

NOT ASSESSED: shroud, and yggdrasil-as-overlay. Yggdrasil appears in our own metrics as
bifrost_yggdrasil_accelerator_memory_used_bytes, so it reads as the GPU service rather than the mesh
network of the same name. If either is doing overlay networking that changes the transport question
materially and should be looked at before deciding.
REFINED (Avery): IPFS as a PULL-THROUGH EDGE CACHE, not on every node - see the BurnBag bead for the full note. Removes objections 1 and 4 substantially: the announce surface shrinks to a known tier, and leaf machines including CNC controllers stay clients rather than peers. Destruction (objection 3) moves out of scope entirely, because destroyable things go to BurnBag instead.

title: Level of detail for the swarm: fleet, agent, detail - one surface per agent, not per action
notes:
REQUIREMENT (Avery, 2026-09-10): "There also needs to be some LoD on downstream. I don't need to see
literally every action, but getting a gist of what things are looking at and working is cool."

This is the level-of-detail rule for the swarm, and it belongs in the design from the start rather
than as a throttle added when the wall starts strobing. It is the same conclusion dock-zqe reached
from the transcript side - "what is worth showing is probably not the transcript text, it is the
derived state" - now stated as a product requirement rather than an implementation note.

WHAT LoD MEANS HERE, concretely: the unit of display is not an ACTION, it is an AGENT'S CURRENT
STATE. One surface per agent, keyed by agent identity so updates route to it rather than creating a
new one, showing what that agent is looking at and whether it is working or blocked. Ten agents is
ten surfaces that change, not a thousand events that scroll.

THE LADDER, coarsest first:
  fleet   - N agents, how many active, how many blocked. One glance, no names.
  agent   - one surface per agent: current artifact, current project, state, last change.
  detail  - the artifact itself, full size. This is where retrieval becomes a real view.
Presence and attention pick the rung: the wall shows `fleet` by default, `agent` for the project
someone is standing in front of, `detail` only for what the human or JARVIS actually opened.

WHY IT IS NOT JUST A FILTER: a coarse rung must still be TRUE. "Three agents working" derived from a
digest that missed events is a confident wrong number, and it is exactly the failure mode
docs/widget-quality.md rule 1 describes. So the digest has to be computed from the agent host's own
complete view (dock-zqe) and carry its own freshness, not sampled from whatever datagrams happened
to arrive.

DEPENDS ON: the digest producer (dock-zqe) for the underlying state, and the retained log for
"agents are quiet" versus "we stopped hearing from them", which are different pictures and must not
render the same.

title: Drive bounded internal origins with headless servoshell over WebDriver - no embedding
notes:
START WITH SERVOSHELL AND WEBDRIVER, NOT WITH EMBEDDING libservo. This is the sequencing that makes
"start today" real, and it sidesteps every cost that made the Servo evaluation say not yet.

What the evaluation verified (docs/servo-and-web-surfaces-decision.md s2a): servo.org/download ships
the servoshell APPLICATION, headless works (SoftwareRenderingContext needs no window and no display
server), servoshell has a WebDriver port (ports/servoshell/webdriver.rs), and
`servo-webdriver-server` 0.5.0 is published as a W3C HTTP server. The evaluation listed the prebuilt
servoshell as a LIMITATION - "the application only, no embedder artifact" - which is true for
embedding and irrelevant here. For driving a bounded set of our own pages over WebDriver, the
application IS the artifact.

WHAT THAT AVOIDS, all of it: the 1.99 GB / ~1,137-crate from-source build on a machine that has
OOM'd; the monthly breaking version bump on a load-bearing dependency; RenderingContext living in a
crate with no semver guarantee; the GL-to-wgpu texture question; and Canvas taking a dependency on
Servo at all. Canvas is not involved. This is an agent-driving lane, not a rendering change.

FIRST RUN, before any of it is wired up:
1. Enumerate the internal origins the agents actually need. Keep it short and explicit; the list IS
   the security boundary.
2. Load each one in headless servoshell and in Chromium. Diff document.body.innerText and a
   screenshot. Read the exact flags from `servoshell --help` rather than trusting any flag name
   written down here.
3. Anything that renders wrong is a bug in OUR app (see dock-ybc.14) - fix it or drop the origin
   from the list. Do not add a compatibility shim.
4. Write the per-target plausibility assertion for each survivor: expected selector present,
   innerText length above a floor, interactive element count. Plus an injected window.onerror and
   unhandledrejection probe, because Servo's console channel only carries what page JS explicitly
   logs and there is no first-class uncaught-exception callback.

Step 4 is not optional garnish. It is the mitigation for the one finding that disqualified Servo for
open browsing, and it is affordable only because the list is short. An origin without a plausibility
assertion is not on the list.

Queue anything that builds behind lockout.
FLAGS NOW VERIFIED, replacing the "read them from --help" hedge above. Read from
ports/servoshell/prefs.rs on servo/servo main:
- `--webdriver` - flag_with_default_parser, DEFAULT PORT 7000, help string "Start remote WebDriver
  server on port". Backed by `webdriver_port: Cell<Option<u16>>` on the shell state, documented as
  "None to disable WebDriver or Some with a port number to start a server to listen to remote
  WebDriver commands".
- `--headless` - `headless: bool`, defaults false.

So the starting command is literally:
    servoshell --headless --webdriver=7000
and then any W3C WebDriver client speaks to localhost:7000. Nothing is built, nothing is embedded,
and Canvas is untouched.

One thing that will bite in headless mode: prefs.rs guards `cmd_args.headless && preferences
.media_glvideo_enabled`, which is a reminder that the headless pref matrix differs from the
windowed one. Combined with the default-OFF list the evaluation found - IndexedDB, service workers,
IntersectionObserver, WebGL2, WebGPU, WebRTC, Web Animations, adoptedStyleSheets, OffscreenCanvas,
Credential Management, and accessibility_enabled - assume the embedded default configuration is
WORSE than the published 66-74% WPT numbers until the matrix is constructed deliberately. Build the
pref matrix as part of step 2 and check it into the repo next to the origin list; it is as much a
part of the security boundary as the list itself.

title: Gate real credentials behind an external review of the crypto design
notes:
GATE, not a nice-to-have. An unaudited vault is unadoptable by anyone serious, and more importantly
we should not point our own real credentials at one. Budget a third-party cryptographic review as a
line item with a date, not an aspiration.

WHAT GATES WHAT:
- Before OUR OWN production credentials move in: the design doc from dock-ybc.12.1 and .12.2
  reviewed by someone who was not in the room, plus the export round-trip green in CI.
- Before any FPL Cloud company's credentials: external audit of the key hierarchy and the
  authenticator's origin binding, published.
- Before any claim about the security properties appears in writing anywhere customer-facing: the
  audit exists and says so. See the overclaim warning on the parent - the E2E boundary is
  user-to-host, not user-to-server, and that must be stated correctly in whatever the audit reviews.

Tenet 9 says prefer self-validating systems over human review gates, and this is the deliberate
exception: WPT for the authenticator and property tests for the crypto envelope ARE the
self-validating part, and the audit exists to catch the class of error tests cannot - a design that
is internally consistent and wrong.

title: Be the authenticator, not just a relying party - passkey-authenticator is Apache-2.0
notes:
BE THE AUTHENTICATOR, not just a relying party. The distinction is the whole product and it is easy
to conflate:
- RELYING PARTY - our services accept passkey login. Easy, solved, `webauthn-rs` (MPL-2.0, kanidm,
  706 stars) is the mature choice. Worth doing, not differentiating.
- AUTHENTICATOR - our vault IS the passkey. This is the one that matters, and it is why an agent can
  be handed a login without ever being handed a credential.

VERIFIED TODAY: 1Password publishes `passkey-authenticator` 0.5.0 (github.com/1Password/passkey-rs,
Apache-2.0 repo, crates MIT OR Apache-2.0, pushed 2026-09-09, actively maintained). The software
authenticator half of this exists under exactly the licence we want. We are not implementing CTAP
from scratch, which was the part that looked hardest.

WHY IT IS THE SAFETY ARGUMENT AND NOT JUST A FEATURE: when we are the authenticator, WE evaluate the
RP ID against the origin. An agent under prompt injection that navigates to a lookalike origin gets
a REFUSAL, not a credential - the binding is cryptographic, not an allowlist we maintain and might
get wrong. That is the property TOTP cannot have at any price, and it is what makes agent-driven
login defensible rather than reckless.

CARRY THE WARNING FROM dock-ybc.13 UNCHANGED: origin binding is small code and the entire security
property. A subtly wrong implementation claims unphishable credentials without enforcing them, which
is worse than having none because we would trust it more. The bar is the WebAuthn WPT suite, and it
does not move because the crate is someone else's.

NOTE THE OVERLAP WITH dock-ybc.13: if we own an authenticator, the "host performs the assertion
out-of-band" option in that bead stops being a workaround and becomes the design. The browser only
needs to reach OUR authenticator - which is a much smaller ask of any engine than full in-engine
WebAuthn, and it partly decouples this from the Servo question.

title: Make export/import a tested contract, not a feature - round-trip in CI
notes:
Avery named this as half the pitch: "Apache-2.0 + Easy export/import." It is the cheapest thing to
build and the most credible thing to promise, because it is the promise incumbents cannot make
sincerely - their business model depends on stickiness.

BUT A PROMISE OF EASY EXPORT THAT SILENTLY ROTS IS WORSE THAN NOT PROMISING IT. So export is not a
feature, it is a TESTED CONTRACT (tenets 6 and 12):
- A round-trip property test: generate a vault with every item type, export, import into a fresh
  instance, assert deep equality including TOTP seeds, custom fields, attachments and SHARING
  STRUCTURE. Sharing is the one that will quietly not round-trip.
- IMPORT from the formats people are actually leaving: Bitwarden JSON (encrypted and plaintext),
  1Password 1pux, Authy (deliberately painful to leave - and Avery is leaving it, which makes this
  the first real test case), Chrome/Safari CSV, KeePass KDBX.
- The round-trip test runs in CI on every commit. The day it fails, export is broken, and that is a
  release blocker rather than a support ticket.
- Export must be usable WITHOUT our client - documented format, plain crypto, a decrypt script in
  the repo. "You can leave" is only true if leaving does not require the thing you are leaving.

Do the Authy import early. It is the concrete migration Avery has been meaning to make, which makes
it the honest first test rather than a hypothetical.

title: Run the blitz-html spike once - it is finished and has never been executed
notes:
spikes/blitz-html/src/main.rs is a finished ~150-line program - usage string, `tera` and `shot`
subcommands, timing instrumentation, PNG output - whose `shot` path parses HTML through
blitz-html/blitz-dom, paints into an anyrender scene and rasterises to RGBA8 via vello_cpu with NO
WINDOW EVER CREATED. That is exactly the Vec<u8> that iced's `Handle::from_rgba` consumes, which
crates/canvas/src/main.rs already uses at four sites.

`out/` is empty. It has never been run. One command against fixtures/css-probe.html answers the
"web surfaces in Canvas" question for the cost of running a binary somebody already wrote.

CORRECTION TO AN EARLIER NOTE: one research pass reported this spike's main.rs as a one-line stub.
It is not - verified by reading the file. The spike is finished and unexercised.

FALSIFIABLE BOTH WAYS: if the buffer comes back correct and fast enough, need 2 is closed against a
dependency with no JS engine and no monthly breaking bump. If it is too slow or the CSS is wrong,
that is a real finding and it cost nothing.

DO NOT adopt Blitz into crates/canvas before this has been run once - it is 0.3.0-beta.2, and the
spike is detached from the workspace on purpose. Keep it that way until there is an output file to
look at.

Also worth knowing, because it removes a false discriminator: "Canvas composites into a wgpu scene,
so a renderer must produce a texture" is already solved in this tree without any engine. The adopted
pattern for a foreign renderer's pixels is pdftoppm - an out-of-process rasteriser producing RGBA,
keyed by sha256 in media.rs, uploaded through iced's image pipeline. ANYTHING emitting RGBA8 is
already compositable. That is not a Blitz property or a Servo property, and it means a captured
Chromium viewport composites by the same path.
RUN. Executed 2026-09-10 at commit ea44bda. Build: 11m45s cold for 312 crates
(dev profile, opt-level 2 on deps); target dir 882MB.

Render path works exactly as this bead predicted. blitz-html -> blitz-dom ->
blitz-paint -> anyrender_vello_cpu ImageRenderer::render_to_vec gives a plain
RGBA8 Vec<u8> with NO WINDOW EVER CREATED. Timings, warm binary, ~384dpi:
  A6 packing slip  1406x1568  416ms (first run, includes font enumeration)
  A4 invoice       2751x3477  116ms
  css-probe.html    710x1080  114ms
That is comfortably inside a live-preview budget, and iced
image::Handle::from_rgba(w, h, pixels) consumes the Vec directly.

Wrinkle worth knowing: anyrender_vello (the GPU backend) requires wgpu ^29 at
every published version back to 0.10, and Canvas/iced 0.14 is on wgpu 27.0.1.
So the zero-copy shared-device path is NOT available today. It does not matter,
because the integration point is a pixel buffer, not a wgpu Texture.

Artifacts under spikes/blitz-html/out/ (gitignored): blitz.png, invoice.png,
plus the WeasyPrint renders of the identical HTML for side-by-side.
close_reason: Spike executed; results recorded on this bead and on dock-ybc.9

title: Give each agent an isolated browser via playwright --isolated, not a new engine
notes:
THE PER-AGENT BROWSING LANE IS A CONFIG CHANGE, NOT AN ENGINE. This is the finding that removes
Servo's strongest leg (docs/servo-and-web-surfaces-decision.md s4).

What per-agent browsing genuinely buys is THE COOKIE JAR. claude-in-chrome's MCP tab group lives in
the human's Brave `Default` profile - Cookies 1.0 MB, written today, next to a `Login Data` store.
An agent navigating anywhere the human is logged in arrives already authenticated AS THEM and can
read the page. The telling detail: this session's permission classifier BLOCKED an agent from
copying that cookie DB for analysis, while the browser tools hand an agent live use of it with no
equivalent check. Exposure is near zero today only because 57 of 59 recorded navigations were to
localhost - one behaviour change away from mattering.

Playwright already solves it and is already adopted here. Every FPL Playwright call site launches a
fresh isolated headless Chromium and never touches the user's browser:
coherence/scripts/verify-workbench-browser.mjs, coherence/scripts/prove-time-series.mjs,
fpl-auth/tests/{companies,design,google,billing}-browser.mjs, jarvis/tests/enrollment_browser.mjs,
fab/scripts/test-console.mjs. ~/Library/Caches/ms-playwright holds chromium-1187 and
chromium_headless_shell-1228. Playwright MCP ships `--isolated` for exactly this. Tenets 10 and 11.

ALSO DROP THE CONTENTION ARGUMENT. There is not one instance in six weeks of two independent agents
driving a browser simultaneously; the three apparent overlaps are all artifacts (a subagent nested
under its parent with identical 28/28 calls, and two fork/resumes - one pair shares 85 of 144
toolu_ ids and starts at the same millisecond). And claude-in-chrome already isolates at the tab
level: tabs_create_mcp creates "a new empty tab in the MCP tab group", navigate acts on "the first
tab in the session's group".

FIRST EXPERIMENT, an afternoon, no build, no dependency: take one real page the agents need that is
NOT localhost and has a login behind it. Drive it through a fresh `playwright --isolated` headless
Chromium and capture innerText, the AX snapshot and a screenshot; drive the same URL through
claude-in-chrome in the human's profile; diff the three.
FALSIFIABLE BOTH WAYS: if the isolated instance reaches the page and snapshots usefully, need 1 is
closed by config. If it CANNOT because the auth lives in the human's profile, that is the real
product question surfacing - agent browsing that requires the human's identity is not isolatable by
any engine, Servo included, and the answer is a service credential, not a browser.

ONE THING TO CHECK BEFORE CITING THIS: whether claude-in-chrome's MCP tab group is scoped per
session or per machine rests on schema text ("the session's group"), not on observed behaviour.

title: Remove the browsermcp connector: nine live processes, zero calls in six weeks
notes:
MEASURED, over all 581 transcripts under ~/.claude/projects, 28 Jul - 8 Sep 2026:
  browsermcp calls: 0. Sessions: 0. Ever.
Meanwhile NINE `fpl-desktop-bridge connect --connector browsermcp` processes from nine distinct
ttys are running right now, all fanning into one mcp-proxy and one node process. Nine processes for
a capability that has never once been invoked.

That is textbook tenet-11 sprawl: moving parts that must be audited, secured and kept alive, earning
nothing. It also has a human gate ("click Connect in the toolbar") that nothing else needs.

WHAT AGENTS ACTUALLY USE instead, same corpus: claude-in-chrome 302 calls / 10 sessions, WebFetch
452 / 40, WebSearch 280 / 37.

BEFORE DELETING, verify the corpus is complete: Codex registers its own native messaging host and
its transcripts are NOT under ~/.claude/projects, so "zero calls" is proven for Claude Code only.
Confirm nothing outside that tree depends on it, then remove the connector and the nine processes.

Deliberately kept OUT of the Servo decision (docs/servo-and-web-surfaces-decision.md) - it is a
cleanup that stands on its own evidence and should not ride on an engine choice.

title: Decide whether agent browsing is a bounded surface or open-ended - it decides the engine
notes:
THE QUESTION THAT DECIDES SERVO, and no further engine research settles it. From
docs/servo-and-web-surfaces-decision.md s8.

If the agent's browsing surface is BOUNDED - our own docs, rustdoc, one vendor's API reference, a
known allowlist - then Servo's compatibility risk collapses to something measured once and pinned,
and Servo at 83.6% DOM parity on static-ish content is already fine for that. Servo becomes viable
far sooner than the quarterly gates suggest.

If the surface is "whatever the agent decides to look at", Servo today is WORSE THAN NO BROWSER.
Not because pages fail - they load fine, over modern TLS and HTTP/2 - but because of HOW they fail:
of the harness tests Chrome passes and Servo fails completely, every single one reports WPT status
`O` (harness OK). No crash, no timeout, no error. The script ran to completion and every assertion
was wrong. The runtime shape is a TypeError inside page JS that halts one script and leaves a
PARTIALLY BUILT DOM - a page that is merely shorter than it should be. An agent reading that has no
signal separating "this dashboard shows no alerts" from "the fetch that populates alerts threw", and
will report the first. That is docs/widget-quality.md rule 1 relocated one level up: fabricated data
presented as real, and a tool that refuses is strictly better than a tool that lies.

So: what is the agent allowed to browse? Answer that and the engine question answers itself.
ANSWERED (Avery, 2026-09-10): BOUNDED, to start. Agent browsing begins on origins we own - fpl
login, enrollment, our own consoles - with SSO handled by injecting a session rather than by driving
a login form.

THIS IS EXACTLY THE TRIGGER docs/servo-and-web-surfaces-decision.md s8 named as the one thing that
would flip the decision early: "if agent browsing is scoped to a known, bounded set of origins the
compat risk collapses to something you measure once and allowlist, and Servo at 83.6% DOM parity on
static-ish content is fine for that today." It has fired. Servo moves from "not yet" to "yes, on
this list", and the four quarterly gates in dock-ybc.17 become the test for LEAVING the list, not
for starting.

AND THE BOUNDED SET INVERTS THE TWO THINGS THAT DISQUALIFIED SERVO:
- Silent failure (11.4% of the tests Chrome passes fail with harness OK - a partially built DOM the
  agent reads as truth) was fatal because a per-target plausibility check "erodes the cost argument"
  across the open web. For eight or ten internal origins, per-target checks are an afternoon. The
  disqualifier becomes affordable precisely because the set is small.
- Web compatibility stops being a risk and becomes A SPEC WE OWN. If our console does not render in
  Servo, we fix OUR console. "Internal tools must render in Servo" is a progressive-enhancement
  discipline that is independently good for accessibility and no-JS resilience. Nobody else's
  roadmap is involved.

WHAT STAYS OUT OF THE SET: vendor portals, dashboards we do not control, anything where a shorter
page could be mistaken for a true one and we cannot fix the page. Those keep the isolated-Chromium
lane (dock-ybc.16) and the credential broker (dock-ybc.12). The split is clean and worth naming:
SERVO FOR WHAT WE OWN THE APP, CHROMIUM FOR WHAT WE OWN ONLY THE CREDENTIAL. Neither has to be
universal, which is why both are affordable.
close_reason: Closed

title: canvas: assert in CI that no dependency turns iced's default features back on
notes:
A NEAR MISS WORTH A GUARD RAIL. The charting evaluation initially recommended `iced_plot 0.5.0`.
Reading its published manifest killed it: crates.io's dependency API shows `iced ^0.14, optional
false, DEFAULT_FEATURES TRUE, features ["advanced"]` - on the UMBRELLA crate.

iced-0.14.0/Cargo.toml: `default = ["wgpu","tiny-skia","crisp","web-colors","thread-pool",
"linux-theme-detection","x11","wayland"]`. Cargo unifies features ADDITIVELY across the graph, so
one dependency declaring default-features on the umbrella overrides Canvas's own deliberate
`default-features = false`.

WHAT THAT WOULD HAVE DONE: iced_graphics-0.14.0/src/color.rs:26-47 shows `web-colors` flips
GAMMA_CORRECTION from true to false, so `pack()` ships raw non-linear sRGB to the shader instead of
`color.into_linear()`. Every colour on the wall composites differently - on top of the OKLCH work -
with NO COMPILE ERROR AND NO FAILING TEST. `crisp` similarly flips `snap` globally
(iced_core-0.14.0/src/renderer.rs:99), and `tiny-skia` compiles a second renderer backend on a
machine that has already OOM'd.

THE RULE: for any iced-family dependency, read the published Cargo.toml.orig from static.crates.io
and read the `default_features` column, not just the crate names.

THE GUARD: a cheap CI assertion that the resolved graph has iced_graphics WITHOUT `web-colors` (and
without `crisp`/`tiny-skia`). `cargo tree -e features` or a small check over `cargo metadata`.
Tenet 12 - this failure mode is silent by construction, so it needs a loud check.
close_reason: Closed

title: canvas-widgets: heatmap has no colour scale - the image cannot be read back to values
notes:
A heatmap without a colour scale is a picture, not a reading. HeatmapProgram (live.rs:1231) renders
cells but publishes no mapping from colour to value, so the viewer cannot recover a number from the
image. Same class of defect as an unlabelled axis (see the sibling bead), and the same rule in
docs/widget-quality.md.

Needs the OKLCH ramp already in live.rs (series_colors, :1007) sampled at N stops, drawn as a
gradient strip with min/mid/max labelled via `fill_text` - which HeatmapProgram already calls at
:1266, so the machinery is in the same function.

NO CANDIDATE SUPPLIED THIS. plotters has no matrix chart type and no colour-scale legend element;
adopting it would have left this exactly where it is. Recorded in
docs/charting-dependency-decision.md.
ENDORSED by Avery 2026-09-10 alongside the P0 cache work: "38-41 also worth taking." Scheduled, not speculative.

title: canvas-widgets: the five chart-shaped programs draw no text - no tick values, no in-plot legend
notes:
VERIFIED: live.rs has exactly six `fill_text` call sites (1266, 1276, 1330, 1379, 1437, 1490), all
of them inside Heatmap, RankedBar, StackedBar, StateTimeline and BurnRate. The five chart-shaped
programs draw NO TEXT AT ALL: SparklineProgram (1668), GaugeProgram (1706), HistogramProgram (1742),
TimeSeriesProgram (1787), ChartProgram (1896).

So the gap is worse than "no tick values" - those plots have no glyphs of any kind. A reader cannot
tell whether a line is at 3 or 3000, which fails the "legible at a glance" rule in
docs/widget-quality.md.

WORK: nice-range tick selection (the standard 1/2/5 x 10^n ladder), a unit-aware formatter, and
about six `fill_text` calls per program - reusing the pattern HeatmapProgram already contains at
live.rs:1266. Roughly 150-250 lines total across the five.

A CORRECTION worth carrying: the earlier aesthetics audit said "no legends". Partly wrong. A legend
DOES exist as an iced `row` outside the canvas (live.rs:118, wired at :142, tested at :2148). The
real finding is narrower - no IN-PLOT legend, and none on the kinds that need one most.

No dependency buys this. See docs/charting-dependency-decision.md: plotters-iced2 is the only
iced-0.14-compatible charting candidate and it still cannot draw Gauge, StateTimeline, SloBurnRate
or a heatmap colour scale.
ENDORSED by Avery 2026-09-10 alongside the P0 cache work: "38-41 also worth taking." Scheduled, not speculative.

title: Decide how WebAuthn reaches an owned browser: upstream to Servo, or host-side assertion
notes:
OUTSTANDING DECISION, blocking passkeys in an owned browser. Both engines are MPL-2.0, so there is no
licensing obstacle to using or contributing to either. The question is how WebAuthn gets there and
who maintains it.

CORRECTION OF A COMMON CONFLATION, because the decision rests on it: Firefox runs on GECKO, not
Servo. Servo was a separate Rust research engine; components went the other way - Stylo (CSS) and
WebRender (GPU) were ported OUT of Servo INTO Gecko under Project Quantum. So Firefox's WebAuthn
lives in Gecko and says nothing about Servo's. A useful corollary: Blitz builds on Stylo, so Blitz
genuinely runs the CSS engine that ships in Firefox.

WHAT THE WORK IS, by layer:
- CTAP2 transport to authenticators (USB HID, platform, hybrid) - LARGELY SOLVED. authenticator-rs is
  Mozilla's own Rust CTAP crate, used by Firefox, same licence. The part that looks hardest is not.
- navigator.credentials JS API surface and DOM bindings - real, engine-specific work.
- RP ID / ORIGIN BINDING VALIDATION - small code, and the entire security property.
- User verification and presence gestures, secure-context and same-origin enforcement.

WHY "SAFELY" IS THE WHOLE QUESTION. The argument for passkeys is that origin binding is enforced
cryptographically rather than by an allowlist we might get wrong. A subtly wrong implementation
inverts that: a browser that CLAIMS unphishable credentials without enforcing them, which we would
trust MORE than passwords precisely because of the claim. False confidence with high stakes - the
same failure shape as a widget rendering fabricated data.

THE BAR IS THEREFORE OBJECTIVE, not "works in testing": the WebAuthn Web Platform Tests. An
implementation that cannot clear WPT does not support the safety argument and must not be treated as
if it does.

THE OPTIONS:
A. Implement in Servo and UPSTREAM it. Review from people who know the engine, shared maintenance,
   and the security-critical part is not maintained solely by us. Slower to land.
B. Fork and maintain ourselves. Rejected on its face: that is not adopting a dependency, it is owning
   a browser's security surface forever.
C. HOST-SIDE OUT-OF-BAND ASSERTION. Do not implement WebAuthn in the browser at all. The host already
   knows which origin the browser navigated to, holds the authenticator, and mediates credentials, so
   it can perform the assertion itself. Non-standard, and sites expect navigator.credentials - but it
   moves origin validation into a small auditable surface we control rather than a full engine
   integration. Worth costing honestly rather than dismissing.

SEQUENCING: this only matters if the Servo evaluation concludes embedding and web-compat are viable.
If an agent hits broken pages constantly, WebAuthn support is moot. Do not scope this until that
result lands.
DIRECTION SET (Avery, 2026-09-10): upstream is the long-term call, but start the fork and
implementation now, for testing. Not literally today - the point is that the two are not sequential.

That resolves the option list above in a way none of the three options captured on its own, and it
is the right shape. Implementing in a fork is how you find out what upstreaming costs; you cannot
write the RFC honestly without having built the thing. The fork is the WORKBENCH, not the product.
What that commits us to:
- Build against the fork, keep the diff rebaseable, and never let anything in Canvas depend on
  fork-only behaviour. The moment a Canvas feature needs a patch that is not upstreamable, the fork
  has stopped being a workbench.
- The bar does not move because it is a fork: WebAuthn WPT still decides. A fork that passes nothing
  is a testbed, which is fine, as long as nobody points a real credential at it.
- Upstream early and in pieces. CTAP transport via authenticator-rs, then the DOM surface, then
  origin binding - rather than one large drop nobody can review.

SEQUENCING CHANGED, and it is the thing to read before scheduling any of this. The Servo evaluation
finished (docs/servo-and-web-surfaces-decision.md) and its answer is NOT YET, on distribution rather
than on the API: every monthly release is a breaking version bump by stated policy, several of the
crates Canvas would integrate against carry no semver guarantee at all, there is no prebuilt
embedder artifact (so Canvas builds Servo from source - 1.99 GB, ~1,137 crates), and Verso, the
project that made embedding look ergonomic, was archived 2025-10-08. It also found Servo cannot host
two instances in one process, so per-agent isolation forces process-per-agent anyway.

So this bead is not blocked on "does Servo work" - it is downstream of Servo being adopted at all,
and today it is not. Keep the decision recorded; do not schedule the implementation until the Servo
trigger in that doc fires.

title: canvas-metrics: bursty sends drop snapshots with ENOBUFS
notes:
Observed live 2026-09-09: canvas-metrics writes all 21 snapshots to stream.sock back to back, and the datagram socket's buffer overruns. Two of three consecutive runs reported 'cannot reach Canvas (No buffer space available (os error 55))' - once for 2 of 21 sends, once for 0. Intermittent, load-dependent, and it silently loses whichever widgets lost the race.

Not a Canvas-side bug: stream_binding's receive loop drains as fast as it can, but a burst of 21 datagrams from a single writer can outrun it, and AF_UNIX SOCK_DGRAM has no flow control. The 2048-byte per-datagram limit already discovered (net.local.dgram.maxdgram) is a separate constraint - this is total buffer, not message size.

Fix belongs in the sender:
- Pace the burst. A few milliseconds between datagrams costs nothing at a 30s
  poll interval and removes the overrun entirely.
- Retry on ENOBUFS with a short backoff rather than dropping the snapshot. The
  error is transient by definition - the receiver drains continuously.
- Keep it loud. The current behaviour already prints rather than swallowing,
  which is right; a retry must not make it silent instead.

Worth noting the shape: a widget whose snapshot is dropped keeps its PREVIOUS value and stays state=ready, so it reads as current while being stale - which docs/widget-quality.md rule 2 is specifically about. Dropping a snapshot is not visually distinguishable from nothing having changed, which is what makes this worse than a loud failure.

Same fix will be needed in canvas-sse, which mirrors this crate's send path.
close_reason: Closed

title: Spike: can a Stylo/Blitz-class renderer serve both Canvas surfaces and doc-forge
notes:
Timeboxed spike, not an implementation. Answer whether one Rust HTML+CSS engine can serve two consumers that both need it today.

CONSUMER 1 - Canvas: render article bodies, documents and briefings inside a
surface, composited into the wgpu scene rather than opened in an external
browser. See the parent bead for why a system webview is ruled out (native
window, not a texture).

CONSUMER 2 - doc-forge (~/src/fpl/doc-forge): a Rust service that shells out to
WeasyPrint for HTML+CSS rendering (22 references) alongside Pandoc (32) and
XeLaTeX (2). WeasyPrint is a Python dependency baked into a 14-step Docker image
together with TeX Live and bundled fonts.

QUESTIONS, in order of what would kill the idea fastest:
1. Does Blitz render into a wgpu texture Canvas can composite, or does it insist
   on owning a window or surface? Pass/fail for consumer 1.
2. What is the CSS coverage against the actual templates doc-forge ships
   (fixtures/, gsg_thermal_packing_slip)? Stylo is mature, but a letterhead that
   renders 95% correctly is a letterhead that cannot be sent to a client.
3. Build and compile cost. A cold canvas build here already takes 12-15 minutes
   under contention.
4. Failure mode on content it cannot render - must disclose rather than showing
   a blank surface (docs/widget-quality.md rule 3).

THE LIKELY ANSWER, worth testing rather than assuming: a SPLIT.
Blitz for PREVIEW - live in Canvas, fast, approximate, and honest about being
approximate. WeasyPrint/LaTeX for FINAL OUTPUT - because PDF needs real vector
text that is selectable, searchable and accessible, and a wgpu rasteriser
produces pixels. Rasterised text in a client-facing PDF is a regression no
amount of speed pays for.

If that split holds, the win is a live preview of doc-forge templates inside
Canvas from the same HTML+CSS source, not the removal of WeasyPrint.

Deliverable: a written answer to the four questions with evidence, and a
recommendation. No production code.
NARROWED, and this removes the spike's biggest risk.

The fast path is not 'embed a browser'. It is TEMPLATES + JSON -> RENDER. That is already how doc-forge works (Tera templates plus data), so both consumers converge on the same shape rather than two.

What the narrowing kills:
- CSS coverage against ARBITRARY web content was the hardest question and the
  most likely reason to abandon this. Against templates WE OWN it becomes a
  bounded, enumerable, testable set - render every template in the repo and diff
  against the WeasyPrint output.
- No JavaScript needed at all.
- No untrusted content, so the security argument against a JS engine and the
  sensitivity concern about rendering the open web beside a dashboard both
  disappear for this path.

Question 2 in the spike should therefore be rewritten: not 'what is Stylo's CSS
coverage' but 'does every template doc-forge ships render identically enough to
its WeasyPrint output to be useful as a preview'. That is answerable in an
afternoon with a fixture diff, and it fails cheaply.

Arbitrary web rendering remains a separate, later question - it is what an RSS
article body would need (dock-4s7) and it carries all the risk this path avoids.
ANSWERED by the spike run at commit ea44bda. THE SPLIT HOLDS, and there is one
blocker on the preview half that this bead did not anticipate.

Q1 wgpu texture or window? -- PASS, via buffer not texture. Headless
render_to_vec returns RGBA8; no window, no surface. iced's Handle::from_rgba
takes it as-is. anyrender_vello wants wgpu ^29 vs Canvas's 27, so the shared-
device path is closed, but the CPU backend makes that irrelevant.

Q2 CSS coverage vs the real templates -- 20/25 pixel-asserted probes pass,
including mm units, flex, grid (%, repeat/minmax, 1/-1), border-radius, dashed
borders, var(), ::before content, :not(:last-child), text-transform,
letter-spacing, position:absolute, gradients, opacity. The whole doc-forge
corpus is only 81 distinct properties, 1 at-rule and 6 pseudo forms, so this is
an enumerable surface, as expected.

  BLOCKER: Blitz paints a phantom heavy black grid on EVERY table and clips the
  rightmost column's value. Confirmed not a stylesheet issue -- it reproduces
  with plain divs using display:table and survives an explicit `border: none`.
  Upstream DioxusLabs/blitz#504 "Collapsed table borders paint a phantom 3px
  grid for borderless tables", still OPEN, along with #638/#793/#422. Every
  doc-forge document template is built on a line-item table, so today the
  preview is wrong in exactly the place a reviewer looks first.

  No @page and no pagination whatsoever: zero hits for @page/PageRule/paginate/
  page_break in blitz-dom. A preview must shim page geometry itself.

Q3 build cost -- 312 crates, 11m45s cold under contention, 882MB target.

Q4 failure disclosure -- Blitz drops unsupported declarations SILENTLY.
blitz-dom/src/document.rs:1171 passes None for stylo's
`error_reporter: Option<&dyn ParseErrorReporter>`. The hook exists one argument
away, so a self-disclosing preview (widget-quality rule 3) is cheap to build.

SURPRISE, worth carrying forward: WeasyPrint is not the faithful reference we
assumed. Run over doc-forge's own stylesheets it silently drops box-shadow
(4 uses in gsg_catalog/gsg_sales_docs), backdrop-filter (1) and
word-break:break-word (7 in the production thermal letterhead). Blitz/Stylo
implements all of those. So a Blitz preview would show shadows the shipped PDF
does not have -- the preview is richer than the artifact, not poorer. Any
preview needs to suppress what WeasyPrint cannot draw, not just match it.

title: Canvas: a runnable demo harness that plays each beat with annotation
notes:
A single command that walks through every animation and beat in sequence, annotated, so they can be watched and critiqued without staging a real demo or waiting for real events.

Motivation: animations and wake sequences are the parts that cannot be reviewed from a diff. Feedback needs to be on the moving thing, and today the only way to see a wake sequence is to actually leave the room and come back.

Requirements that decide whether this is useful or misleading:

- DRIVE THE REAL PATH. Each beat must be triggered through the same control
  socket, stream contract and animation code the real system uses, never a
  bespoke mock. A harness that reimplements the animation gives feedback on the
  harness. Where a real trigger is unavailable (presence, for instance), inject
  the real EVENT rather than calling the renderer directly.
- ANNOTATE ON SCREEN. Each beat states what it is, what triggered it, and what
  is being demonstrated, so a critique is about the right thing. Annotation
  should be visibly an overlay, not mistaken for part of the design.
- PAUSE, REPLAY, STEP. Feedback needs a second look at the thing that felt
  wrong. Views already carry SourcePosition { Live, Sequence } (view.rs:47),
  which is the same replay idea.
- REPORT TIMINGS. Show frames-per-second and elapsed time for each beat, since
  the difference between a power move and a loading screen is measured in
  hundreds of milliseconds and cannot be judged reliably by eye.

Beats to cover: wake on arrival (logo, surfaces flying in, greeting), sleep and
screensaver descent, each of the ten shaders, view snap and fit (Ctrl-Option-L /
Ctrl-Option-F), display reflow on monitor change, widget data states including
demo, stale and no-data, the briefing pacing, and a spec build progressing.

This is also the natural home for the honesty checks: a beat that renders
fabricated data should be visibly labelled DEMO in the harness exactly as it
would be in production, per docs/widget-quality.md rule 1. If the harness is
allowed to fake things the product may not, it will teach the wrong lesson.

title: Canvas: per-zone wake policy over presence, face and voice evidence
notes:
dock-cdz already renders zone-aware presence with three independent evidence channels - Presence, Face, Voice - and keeps missing or stale evidence visibly unknown. That is the substrate. This is the POLICY on top: which combination of evidence wakes a screen, and why it differs by room.

THE ASYMMETRY THAT MAKES THIS PER-ZONE: the cost of each error is not the same
in every room.

- BEDROOM: waking wrongly is much worse than failing to wake. A screen coming on
  at 3am because someone rolled over or talked in their sleep is a real harm.
  So require CONJUNCTION: face in frame AND voice activity. Either alone is not
  enough. Fail closed - ambiguous evidence stays asleep.
- OFFICE / DESK: failing to wake is the worse error. Someone walking up and
  waiting for a screen is friction on every single arrival. Presence alone may
  be sufficient, with identity resolved afterwards for anything sensitive.

Same evidence, opposite thresholds, because the errors are not symmetric. A
single global sensitivity would be wrong in both rooms.

WAKE WORDS as an additional channel: 'Wake up', or a JARVIS address phrase, if
wake-phrase detection is reliable enough to trust. Worth treating as evidence
that RAISES confidence rather than as a bypass - a phrase heard from a TV or a
phone should not wake a bedroom on its own, which is the same conjunction
argument.

PRE-FLIGHT AND POST-BRIEFING, per zone:
- Pre-flight runs before a briefing begins: warm the data plane for what this
  zone is about to show (dock-qwv's prefetch-on-approach), pick the level of
  detail for this screen, and settle audio routing before the first word rather
  than during it.
- Post-briefing decides what the room does afterwards: return to screensaver,
  hold the last view, or dim to ambient. A bedroom almost certainly returns to
  sleep; a desk probably holds. This is a per-zone default, overridable.

SCREENSAVER AS THE SLEEP STATE, not a separate feature: dock-ybc.1's sleep half
and the screensaver are the same thing seen from two directions. An unobserved
screen genuinely stops drawing; the screensaver is what it shows on the way down
and on the way back up. Which shader, and whether it runs at all, is reasonably
a per-zone choice too - a bedroom probably wants something dark and slow or
nothing.

Ownership: publishers own identity semantics and expiry (per dock-cdz); this
policy consumes their evidence and decides wake. Canvas should not become an
identity authority, and equally should not become the place wake rules are
hardcoded - they belong in configuration a person can change per room.

title: Canvas: shared projects with auto-updated per-collaborator briefings
notes:
Invite someone to a project and have them stay current without being managed: CawLaw for family and a colleague, Ohm for one group, Player for another. Each collaborator gets an automatically maintained get-up-to-speed briefing for the projects they can see.

This is the convergence of three beads already filed rather than new machinery:
- dock-8nz: outward links gated on identity (SSO, or facial when enrolled and
  sensitive), so a collaborator opening a link is a verified viewer and
  dock-7pa's sensitivity model applies per-person rather than being bypassed.
- dock-8n5: a briefing is an identity plus a query routed by presence, so 'their
  briefing' is the same mechanism as 'my briefing' with a different identity.
- dock-rk4: the per-project artifact index is what makes 'what changed'
  answerable without someone writing an update by hand.

The design point that keeps this honest: a collaborator's briefing must be
derived from what they are ENTITLED to see, not filtered from a full one after
the fact. Filtering after assembly is how the wrong thing gets shown once - and
once is enough when it is someone's father's legal work.

Alfalfa owns project identity and membership; Canvas should ask rather than
maintain its own list (tenet 2).

title: Canvas: demo-mode latency budget — probe the machine, cache hard, degrade by LoD
notes:
A demo is a latency problem wearing a features costume. Everything below is about the gap between asking and seeing.

- Probe before starting. Check the local machine's GPU and network and pick a
  level of detail accordingly, rather than discovering mid-demo that a shader
  is running at 6fps on a laptop. dock-8nz already frames WASM as a LoD tier;
  this is the same idea applied to the native client.
- Hard-cache everything cacheable. Known briefing audio and known phrases are
  the obvious win - synthesise once, ship the bytes, stream them in during
  loading rather than generating on the spot.
- Pre-research the audience. Prefetch and cache what they are likely to ask
  about, so the happy path is warm. The unhappy path - a genuinely new idea
  with nothing cached - must still work, dynamically, and should be the case
  that gets tested rather than the one that gets hoped for.
- Stream during loading. Anything that shows progress truthfully beats a
  spinner, and the boot sequence has natural cover for prefetch.

Measured facts that bear on this, from 2026-09-09:
- Background shaders are NOT loops and cannot be frame-cached: Star Nest and
  Meme translate through a field indefinitely, and at 5760x1200 a 2-second
  30fps loop would be 1.66 GB of VRAM. FrameClock already supports capping
  max_fps (screensaver.rs:672), which is the real lever. See dock-iuy.
- Three displays showing the same shader is NOT 3x GPU cost - same total
  fragment count as one wide render, only pass setup is tripled. See dock-es5.
- A cold cargo build on this machine takes 12-15 minutes under contention.
  Anything that compiles during a demo is a mistake; ship binaries.

The number that matters is time from 'fpl login' to the greeting, and from a
stated idea to visible progress. Neither is currently measured.

title: Canvas: watch a spec build and deploy live
notes:
A demo beat and a real feature: state a new idea, watch it go from SPEC to deployed in realtime on screen.

This is dock-8cd (agent attention surface) with the stakes raised. The machinery is the same - agents emit what they are doing, Canvas renders it as a spatially stable cluster - but a demo audience is watching, so two things matter more than usual:

- STABILITY over completeness. The clustering rules in dock-8cd exist because a
  window jumping between files is unwatchable. In a demo that is the difference
  between 'the system is working' and 'something is wrong'. Bounded working set,
  LRU with admission resistance, positions that do not move on update.
- HONEST PROGRESS. A spec build that shows a spinner while nothing happens, or
  claims a step succeeded because a command returned 0, is the same class of
  failure as a widget rendering fabricated data. The build view must show what
  actually completed, and Alfalfa already owns spec/run state to derive it from
  (alfalfa_run_tail, alfalfa_spec_coverage).

Four demo domains to support, which mostly differ in what the deployed artifact
is rather than in the pipeline: electronics (kicad, legion-of-bom), website,
research, law.

title: Canvas: briefing surfaces — newcomer intro and recurring executive update
notes:
Two distinct briefing kinds, both rendered as Canvas views:

1. FIRST LAUNCH: an intro briefing that explains what JARVIS, Alfalfa and Canvas
   are and how they relate, ending in 'what would you like to work on?'
2. SUBSEQUENT: an executive update - what changed across the person's projects
   since they last looked. Well paced rather than a dump.

This is dock-8n5 (briefings, approvals, polls as routed artifacts) with its
first concrete consumer, and it should be built as that rather than as a
bespoke slideshow: a briefing is an identity plus a query, rendered as a view,
routed by presence to whatever screen the person is at.

Consequences worth keeping:
- Pacing is a property of the view, not of a script. An executive update that
  cannot be paused, rewound or skipped is a video, and a view already has
  SourcePosition { Live, Sequence } for exactly this (view.rs:47).
- 'Since you last looked' needs a per-person read position, which is the same
  state dock-aqz's unread dots need. One mechanism, two surfaces.
- Auto-updated per-project briefings for shared collaborators is the same query
  with a different identity - see dock-8nz for the identity gate.

Content must respect docs/widget-quality.md: a briefing that renders a metric
with no source behind it is the fabrication rule (rule 1) at presentation
scale, and a demo is precisely where that temptation is strongest.

title: Canvas: wake the screens on arrival, and sleep them when the room is empty
notes:
This is waking the SCREENS, not starting the system. The backend has been running the whole time. Closer to 'wake up, daddy's home' than to a boot.

  presence detects arrival and identifies who it is
  a holographic 3D FPL logo spins up, with SFX and the CRT line opening out
  surfaces fly in from small, expanding outward into place
  JARVIS: 'Good afternoon, Avery. What would you like to work on today?'
  the most recent project, or home, is already there

WHY THIS IS AN ARGUMENT FOR THE ARCHITECTURE, not decoration on top:

The reason it can feel instant is that NOTHING IS STARTING. dock-qwv splits a
control plane that always flows - small, cheap, current whether or not anyone is
watching - from a data plane that only moves to observed screens. While the room
was empty the backend kept state current, so waking only fetches pixels for what
is actually on screen. And because the control plane already knows what a screen
WOULD need, presence detecting approach can warm the data plane before anyone
arrives. The wake is a reveal, not a load. If it ever feels like loading, the
control/data split is not doing its job.

That makes the sleep half real rather than cosmetic: unobserved screens should
genuinely stop drawing - no shader frames, no data plane traffic - which is the
GPU and bandwidth saving presence was meant to buy.

THE ANIMATION, and what already exists for it:

- Surfaces flying in from small is a bounds transition, and crates/canvas/src/
  transition.rs already ships ease_out_cubic, lerp, lerp_rgb, lerp_palette and
  TRANSITION_DURATION = 280ms, already used by main.rs for surface bounds and
  theme swaps. The fly-in is that, from a small rect to the final rect,
  staggered per surface. Do not write a second animation system.
- A holographic 3D spinning logo is a wgpu shader, and the shader path is built:
  screensaver.rs has BackgroundProgram, a uniform struct with res/time/origin,
  ten WGSL shaders and a FrameClock with configurable max_fps. A logo is another
  program on that path rather than new plumbing.
- Stagger and easing carry the whole effect. Everything arriving at once reads
  as a redraw; sequenced arrival reads as intent. Keep the stagger short enough
  that it never becomes a wait - this is the first impression, and a beat too
  long turns a power move into a loading screen.
- 60fps or do not ship it. A logo animation that stutters is worse than no logo
  animation, and dock-iuy already measured the levers: FrameClock max_fps,
  reduced resolution, and the fact that three displays cost the same total
  fragment work as one wide render.

Dependencies, all already filed:
  dock-qwv  backend persists; screens attach, sleep and wake
  dock-7pa  presence distinguishes Detected from Verified, so the greeting knows
            it is Avery rather than merely someone; fail closed when unsure
  dock-blw  displays reflow on reconfiguration, so a screen waking to a changed
            monitor arrangement lands correctly

COLD START is a different and rarer case - first install, or a reboot - and still
needs handling. Canvas enumerates displays once at startup through Dock Control
(main.rs:362), so starting Canvas first latches displays=0 and it renders
nothing, permanently, while still reporting visible=true. Observed 2026-09-09.
Until dock-blw lands, cold start must order Dock Control before Canvas and verify
displays > 0 before showing anything.

Numbers that matter, neither measured today: for wake, presence detected to
first frame. For cold start, fpl login to the greeting.

title: Canvas: per-project sha256 artifact index with provenance, reportable by Alfalfa
notes:
Canvas holds an index of every artifact it has seen or produced, per project, keyed by sha256. Alfalfa queries it, so known work-product is answerable across all projects rather than per repo.

Extends dock-9uy (durable artifacts). Canvas already content-addresses everything it touches - MediaCacheKey, AssetRef.sha256, background_assets keyed by sha256 - so the index is largely bookkeeping over identities that already exist.

THE LOAD-BEARING DISTINCTION is between artifacts that are recreatable from
source and external material worth saving and citing, because it decides what
the store is allowed to forget:

- DERIVED: a rasterized page, a chart from a query, an image from a known
  prompt/model/seed. The bytes are a CACHE. If the recipe and its inputs
  survive, the bytes are recomputable and safe to evict under pressure.
- EXTERNAL: a paper, a datasheet, a customer document. The bytes ARE the source
  of truth. Never evictable without an explicit decision, and they carry a
  citation - where it came from, when it was retrieved, under what terms.
- AUTHORED: made here and not derived from anything. Also not recreatable, also
  never silently evictable.

Two properties fall out:

1. Lineage for free. If a derived artifact names its inputs by sha256, 'what did
   this come from' and 'what depends on this' are answerable without a separate
   graph. Same shape as dock-ev4's agent DAG, applied to work-product.

2. Recreatable becomes CHECKABLE rather than declared. It is not a label someone
   sets, it is a property: recipe complete, inputs still present, tool version
   resolvable. An artifact claiming recreatable whose inputs were evicted is a
   lie the index can detect - the same disclosure discipline as the DEMO badge
   in docs/widget-quality.md rule 1.

Ownership: Canvas holds the index because it already sees the bytes; Alfalfa
reports because it owns project and spec identity. Loose coupling per tenet 2 -
Canvas should not learn to report, and Alfalfa should not learn to cache.

Design notes:
- Citation is a first-class field on External, not a comment. If a briefing
  quotes a paper, the citation should be derivable from the index rather than
  reconstructed by whoever wrote the briefing.
- The index is per project but the store is content-addressed and therefore
  global: the same sha256 referenced by three projects is one blob and three
  index entries. That is also how 'do we already have this' gets answered
  cheaply.
- Retention policy differs by class, so eviction needs the class present before
  it can run at all. Get the classification in from the first write rather than
  backfilling it.
TEMPLATES AS IaC makes 'recreatable' verifiable rather than declared.

This bead says recreatable should be a checkable property - recipe complete, inputs present, tool version resolvable - rather than a label someone sets. Managing templates as infrastructure-as-code supplies the missing half: a template addressed by repo path and git sha is a verifiable recipe, where an uploaded blob is not.

So a derived artifact's recipe becomes concrete:
  template repo + git sha, input data (itself content-addressed), engine version

All three are resolvable, which means the index can PROVE an artifact is
recreatable instead of trusting a flag. An artifact whose template sha no longer
resolves is detectably un-recreatable, and should be reclassified so its bytes
stop being treated as an evictable cache.

It also makes 'regenerate every packing slip with the new letterhead' a query
over the index rather than a migration - find artifacts derived from template X
below sha Y, re-render.

And ownership comes free: if templates live in a git repo governed by OIDC, who
may change a template and who may render with it are the same identity questions
fpl-auth already answers, rather than a new permission system inside the
artifact store.

title: Canvas: briefings, approvals, polls and scheduling as routed artifacts
notes:
Once a view is an identity plus a query, addressable by link and routed by presence, a whole class of interaction collapses into one mechanism: briefings, approvals, scheduling and polls are all an ID, a query, and a rendered view.

What makes this work rather than being another notification system:

- Presence routes it to wherever the person actually is, so a missed link does
  not strand the interaction. The artifact finds the person instead of the
  person finding the artifact. That is the inverse of email.
- Identity is already established by the link gate (dock-8nz), so an approval
  knows who approved without a separate auth step.
- It is a view, so it gets everything views already have: sizing (dock-v7c),
  sensitivity (dock-7pa), provenance and freshness, and reflow onto whatever
  display is available.
- The unread state is already scoped per project by dock-aqz's launcher bar, so
  'you have a briefing' has somewhere to appear that is not a badge on a phone.

Design notes:
- Response is the new part. Canvas is read-only today, and an approval or a poll
  needs a reply path. That is the same interaction contract dock-4s7 (RSS
  click-to-open) and dock-aqz (click-to-jump) both need, so whichever lands
  first should define it - and it must be host-mediated rather than a widget
  performing an action directly.
- An approval is a decision with consequences, so it needs a durable record of
  who decided and when, which points at dock-9uy's durable artifact store rather
  than at ephemeral view state.
- Routing to 'everyone' by presence needs a policy for nobody-is-present: hold
  and deliver on arrival, rather than dropping or broadcasting blindly.

title: Canvas: WASM target so a view can be shared as a link
notes:
Render Canvas in a browser so a view can be sent as a link.

This is largely free IF dock-qwv lands first: once screens are dumb subscribers to a backend, a browser is just another screen with a different renderer. Built before that split, it would be a second port with its own transport and its own copy of the state.

Portability is better than expected. canvas-widgets depends only on serde, serde_json, canvas-core, iced and schemars. The sole non-portable code is render.rs, which spawns a process for static matplotlib PNGs, and one std::fs::read at lib.rs:605 for loading a spec from a path. Both are feature-gatable, so the widget library is essentially wasm-ready.

The host half is cleanly separated in the canvas crate and is what a browser replaces: stream_binding (UnixDatagram), control (Unix socket), terminal (PTY), workspace_store (filesystem), loopback.

Shaders port as-is: they are WGSL and WebGPU speaks WGSL natively.

Scope should be view-only. No terminals, no PTY, no file opening, no window or workspace management - those are host concerns a page cannot have. Transport is a WebSocket or SSE from the backend rather than stream.sock, which is a 2048-byte local datagram and a bad wire protocol.

THE DESIGN QUESTION TO SETTLE FIRST, because two features are about to contradict:

A share link is by definition someone who is not the owner viewing. dock-7pa
blurs or redacts for exactly that case. Ship both naively and either the link is
a wall of redactions, or sharing becomes the exception that defeats the privacy
model everywhere.

Proposed rule: sharing is an explicit publish of named widgets at Public
sensitivity, never a mirror of the current screen. 'Share my view' is the
dangerous framing because a view contains whatever happened to be on it -
including an EyesOnly widget someone opened five minutes ago. Publishing names
what leaves; mirroring cannot.

Unverified: whether iced 0.14 with the wgpu backend builds for
wasm32-unknown-unknown with the feature set Canvas uses. Worth a spike before
committing, since that is the load-bearing assumption.
RESOLUTION, better than the rule proposed above: gate outward links on identity - SSO, or facial when the viewer is enrolled and the content is sensitive.

The earlier rule (publish only Public widgets, never mirror a screen) assumed a share link is anonymous. If the link verifies who is opening it, that constraint dissolves: EyesOnly can mean 'this person', and a link can carry sensitive content safely because the viewer is verified rather than assumed. dock-7pa's sensitivity model then applies per-viewer on a shared link exactly as it does at a wall, with the same fail-closed rule - unverified identity degrades, it does not reveal.

This also makes sharing and privacy one mechanism instead of two that contradict. Presence answers 'who is in front of this screen'; link identity answers 'who opened this'. Same question, two transports.

FRAMING: WASM is a level-of-detail tier for the desktop, not a separate product.
Same document, same widgets, lower fidelity and no host capabilities. That also
puts a mobile client close to free, since it is the same subscriber again with a
smaller viewport and dock-v7c sizing deciding what fits.

title: Canvas: no SSE consumer exists, though three views declare SSE sources
notes:
config/views/elmers-now.json declares sse:elmers/activity, sse:elmers/attention and sse:elmers/state, and operational_views.rs:144 validates 'sse' as a transport. Canvas contains no SSE client: zero matches for event-stream, EventSource or any SSE type across all crates. Those three widgets will sit on Loading indefinitely, exactly as the prometheus:* ones did before canvas-metrics existed.

The bridge half is real and should not be confused with the missing half. fpl-desktop-bridge does SSE properly - proxy.rs:199 detects text/event-stream, render_stream.rs:142 transform_sse rewrites a response stream, and mcp-streamable-http is a first-class connector kind (config.rs:276).

But that SSE is MCP protocol framing: transform_sse takes a request and transforms its response stream. It is transport for tool calls, not a general event feed a dashboard can subscribe to. 'The bridge does SSE' and 'Canvas can subscribe to an event stream through the bridge' are different claims and only the first holds today.

The pattern is already solved once, so this is not new architecture: canvas-metrics is an external process that asks the bridge for authenticated data, normalizes the result, and writes canvas.widget.snapshot.v1 datagrams to stream.sock. An SSE connector is the same programme with a different source, and inherits provenance badging, freshness and sizing for free.

Related: this is the same declared-but-unimplemented shape recorded on dock-cov.3.3, where ContentSource::Stream renders 'Connecting to stream...' forever. Worth checking whether the elmers widgets should say 'no consumer' rather than Loading in the meantime, per docs/widget-quality.md rule 3.
close_reason: Closed

title: Canvas: generated images accumulate as durable project artifacts
notes:
Images an agent generates should appear in the project and stay there, stacking up over time - a created-artifacts shelf per project rather than files that vanish into a scratch directory.

This is dock-9uy applied to a specific, high-value case, and should share its resolver rather than growing a parallel one. An image is an artifact with a preview.

Existing surface: main.rs keeps background_assets keyed by sha256 (main.rs:336) and media.rs already plans, rasterizes, caches and invalidates on resize. Content addressing by sha256 is the right identity for an accumulating shelf - it deduplicates regenerations of the same output for free.

Design questions worth settling early:
- Ordering and retention. Newest first is obvious; what ages out is not.
  Probably nothing ages out automatically, since the value is that they
  accumulate - but then it needs a size budget and a way to prune deliberately.
- Provenance. Per docs/widget-quality.md rule 1 these are generated, and the
  shelf should say which model or run produced each one. That is the same
  disclosure family as Provenance on widget data.
- The shelf is a widget, so it needs dock-v7c sizing and dock-8cd's stability:
  a new image should not reshuffle the ones already there.

title: Canvas: DAG view of agents, per-project and global
notes:
Show edgerunner agents as a graph with their statuses - globally, or scoped to one project.

Half the model exists. MeshNode { id, label, state, detail } and MeshNodeState { Active, Paused, Suspended, Stopped, Hidden } (control.rs:294-315) already describe an agent well, and the doc comments were clearly written with agents in mind: Paused is 'up but its work is paused (agent idle, human gate)'.

What is missing is edges. MeshSnapshot is { nodes: Vec<MeshNode> } (control.rs:319) - a flat list with no relationships, so it can render a status board but not a DAG. Adding edges means deciding what an edge means: spawned-by, blocked-on, or data-dependency. They are different graphs and only the first is unambiguous from an agent runtime.

Layout is the real work. A DAG of live agents relaid out on every status change would violate the stability rule from dock-8cd - motion local, position stable. Node positions should be stable across status changes and only reflow when the graph's shape changes.

Canvas already has canvas_mermaid, which may be the cheapest first cut: render the DAG as mermaid and iterate on whether a bespoke graph widget earns its place.

title: Canvas: stream agent transcripts into per-project clusters
notes:
Tail edgerunner/opencode agent transcripts, parse them, and stream them to Canvas so each project shows what its agents are doing.

Transport exists: stream.sock and StreamEnvelope, the same path canvas-metrics uses. An opencode plugin is the natural producer since it already sits in the agent's loop.

The hard part is volume, not plumbing. Agent transcripts are a genuine firehose, and rendering them raw recreates the strobing dock-8cd exists to prevent. So this must land on the same discipline:
- a bounded working set with LRU, admission resistance and eviction hysteresis
- surfaces keyed by identity (agent, or file) so updates route rather than
  create, and positions stay stable
- salience: which agents earn a slot, not which lines get drawn

What is worth showing is probably not the transcript text. It is the derived
state - what the agent is working on, which files it has touched, whether it is
blocked - which is a small, slowly-changing summary rather than a stream. The
transcript is the source; the surface should be the digest.

Pairs with dock-8cd (files being edited and viewed) and the DAG view: this is
the per-agent detail behind a DAG node.
STATUS 2026-09-10, verified: NOT STARTED. No producer, no contract, no digest.

Note the dependency this bead's own analysis implies but does not state: "the surface should be the
digest, not the transcript" means THE DIGEST HAS TO BE COMPUTED SOMEWHERE, and that somewhere is
almost certainly dock-qwv's backend rather than each screen. Reasons:
- Computing it per screen means every screen tails every transcript, which is the coupling dock-qwv
  exists to remove.
- The digest is small and slowly-changing - exactly the CONTROL PLANE dock-qwv defines, which flows
  regardless of observers. The raw transcript is the data plane and should never leave the agent
  host.
That is a cleaner split than "stream transcripts to Canvas": the agent host digests, the backend
retains, screens subscribe to a summary. It also means the firehose never crosses the network,
which answers the volume problem by construction rather than by throttling.

SALIENCE IS THE OPEN DESIGN QUESTION AND IT IS NOT A RENDERING ONE. "Which agents earn a slot" is a
ranking problem over a changing set, and the honest version has to survive the case where twenty
agents are all busy. Worth deciding whether the ranking is recency, blocked-ness, human-attention
(which project is on screen), or an explicit pin - before any of it is drawn.

title: canvas-widgets: intrinsic minimum and comfortable sizing per widget kind
notes:
Boxes resize, content does not. crates/canvas-widgets/src/live.rs uses Length::Fill 36 times against Length::Fixed 5 and Length::Shrink 0, so every widget stretches to its surface and centres fixed-size content inside. There is no min_size, min_width, preferred_size or intrinsic concept anywhere in canvas-widgets or canvas. NormalizedRect (lib.rs:592) is pure fractions with no floor, so a widget can be placed arbitrarily small and will render an unreadable smear rather than refusing.

media.rs already models intrinsic dimensions for images and PDFs (media.rs:81, 95). The concept exists and was never extended to widgets.

Rules to implement:

1. Minimum is where content stops being READABLE, not where it stops fitting. A
   widget shrunk until its label truncates is already below minimum.

2. Two numbers per kind, not one: min (below this, degrade) and comfortable
   (what layout aims for). Space is precious, so the target is comfortable and
   not 'as large as available'.

3. Size to content; distribute slack in the LAYOUT, not inside the widget. A
   stat gains nothing from doubling in height; a time series gains a lot from
   doubling in width. Leftover space should go to the kinds that convert it into
   information. This is the actual fix for stretched boxes with marooned
   content.

4. Below minimum, degrade down a documented ladder rather than squashing: a stat
   drops footer, then label, then keeps only the value; a chart drops axis
   labels, then gridlines, then becomes a sparkline. Same philosophy as
   SurfaceContent::Unsupported - say less, do not render something misleading.

5. Derive minimums from the type scale rather than hardcoding pixels, or the
   42/47.6/63 problem repeats one layer down. A stat's min height is
   hero + label + footer + 2x padding, computed from ThemeMetrics.

6. Aspect ratio as a preference, not a lock. Charts read best between 4:3 and
   16:9, a sparkline wants 3:1 or wider, a gauge wants roughly square. Prefer,
   do not enforce - quant.rs:243 has a test asserting charts reflow WITHOUT
   preserving intrinsic aspect ratio, so that was a deliberate decision worth
   keeping.

7. Viewing distance scales density. A 3m wall needs larger minimums than a
   laptop. Derivable from display PPI and an assumed distance rather than
   configured, and it composes with dock-blw's reflow, which already recomputes
   on display change.

Rough starting minimums, to be derived rather than pasted: stat ~160x120,
gauge ~120x120 square-ish, time series ~220x110 (a line below about 48px of
plot area is a smear), heatmap needs 6-8px per cell plus label gutter,
table/event log needs header plus three rows to be worth the space.

Ties into dock-8cd: the attention cluster's capacity depends on knowing how
small a file surface can usefully be, so this is a prerequisite for deriving
slot count from display area rather than guessing four.

title: screensaver: uniform slot assumes one instance, breaks with multiple displays
notes:
crates/canvas/src/screensaver.rs:753 keys a shader's uniform slot by shader index, documented as 'each shader appears at most once on screen, which keeps the slot stable without the primitive having to be told who it is.'

That assumption does not hold with more than one display. main.rs:4339 pushes screensaver::view(...) inside fn view(&self, window), which runs per window, so three displays create three BackgroundPrimitive instances for the same shader index sharing one uniform slot.

BackgroundPrimitive is { index, elapsed_seconds } (screensaver.rs:747) with no viewport origin, so each window renders the shader from its own (0,0). Consequences:

1. res is whatever window wrote the slot last. Displays of differing size would
   compute UVs against another display's resolution. Currently masked because
   all three attached displays are 1920x1200 - it would surface immediately on a
   mixed-DPI or mixed-size setup, which is the normal laptop-plus-monitor case.
2. The background is duplicated per display rather than spanning them. Three
   copies of the same shader side by side, not one field across the desk. Fine
   for Star Nest, visibly tiled for anything with large-scale structure.

Fix: key the uniform slot by widget instance rather than by shader, and give the
primitive its window origin and the full desktop extent so a shader can choose
to span or repeat. Spanning versus tiling then becomes a per-shader or per-
workspace choice rather than an accident of the slot allocator.

Cost note for anyone reading this expecting a performance problem: three
displays is not three times the GPU work. 3 x 1920x1200 is the same 6.9M
fragments as one 5760x1200 pass; only pass setup is tripled.
close_reason: Closed

title: Canvas control: no way to set the background shader over the protocol
notes:
The F2 background picker can set Background::Shader { shader_id, speed } (background_picker.rs:87) but the control protocol cannot. There is no command for it:

- SetBackground { path } takes an image path (control.rs:122, 1186)
- ClearBackground resets it
- 'bg' | 'theme' is SetTheme { project_id }, not a background
- 'screensaver_shader' | 'shader' sets Command::ScreensaverShader (main.rs:2904),
  which selects the SCREENSAVER's shader

That last one is the trap. main.rs:4339 renders the visible wallpaper from
document.background's own shader_id, so changing the screensaver index does
nothing to what is on screen while a document shader is pinned. The command
returns 'OK shader=7 (Flame)' either way, which reads exactly like success.

Cost, observed: an agent tried three times tonight to show a shader on screen,
got an affirmative reply each time, and told the human to look at something that
was never going to change. The human had to say 'no flame' twice before the
agent found the actual cause.

Fix: a SetBackgroundShader { shader_id, speed, project } command, and a receipt
that reports the resulting visible background rather than the field that was
written.

Wider point for dock-tiz: anything the UI can do, the protocol should be able to
express. A picker that can reach state the protocol cannot guarantees an agent
will eventually claim to have done something it had no way of doing.
REFRAME: the fix is not a SetBackgroundShader command. The per-project workspace should be managed as a unit, and commands should edit that unit rather than poke adjacent global state.
