Background, theme, layout, views, wallpaper and surfaces are all properties of one thing - the project workspace - and they are already persisted that way (workspaces.json stores a background per project; dock has aurora-drift pinned, fab has spirales). What is missing is that the control protocol treats them as loose independent switches.

That mismatch is exactly what went wrong tonight. 'shader 7' set a screensaver-global index; the visible wallpaper came from the dock workspace's own pinned shader_id; both are 'the background' colloquially, and nothing in either command or reply said which unit it belonged to. Adding a SetBackgroundShader command alongside the others would leave the same shape and just add a fourth switch to confuse.

Better shape, and it already half exists: reconcile.rs takes a DesiredWorkspaceState and computes a patch. Control commands should be sugar that edits the workspace unit and goes through that reconciler, so:
- every mutation names the workspace it edits
- a receipt reports the resulting workspace state, not the field written
- switching projects loads a unit rather than leaving fragments of the previous
  one behind
- saving, restoring and sharing a workspace covers everything about it, because
  the unit is the thing that persists

Loose per-field commands should still exist, for editing the unit's config. They
just should not be the primary interface, and they should be understood as edits
to a named unit rather than as global switches.
close_reason: Closed

title: Canvas: agent artifacts live in the workspace, on durable storage
notes:
Files and artifacts an agent produces or retrieves should land in the workspace rather than in scratch directories only the agent knows about, and be backed by durable storage rather than /private/tmp.

The motivating failure is from tonight and was nearly expensive: three shaders existed only as uncommitted edits in a /private/tmp worktree - no branch, no stash, no dangling commit. macOS purges that directory. They survived because someone remembered them, not because the system kept them. Agent output that lives only in a scratch path is one reboot from gone.

Shape:
- An agent writing an artifact addresses it to a project, not a filesystem path.
  The workspace resolves where it actually lands and keeps it.
- Retrieval is by project plus identity, so a later session finds what an
  earlier one produced without knowing which scratch directory it used.
- Durable means surviving reboot, tmp reaping, and the session that made it.
- The human sees it as a surface in that project, which is what makes it
  discoverable rather than archaeological.

Relationship to the widget artifact model already filed: that packages binder +
widget + source binding as an addressable unit with project-then-global
resolution. This is the same addressing applied to agent working output, and
the two should share one resolver rather than growing two.

Also connects to the attention surface: a PDF an agent is reading and a report
it just wrote are the same kind of thing to a viewer - something the agent
touched, in a project, worth seeing.

title: Canvas: agent attention surface - show what the agent is reading and editing
notes:
When an agent opens a PDF section or edits code, that should appear on screen. 'Your eyes are visible to me.' Across projects it becomes a live indicator of work being done.

Direction matters: the agent must EMIT what it is attending to, not drive Canvas imperatively. Tonight an agent drove the control socket directly, applied a background to a project the human was not looking at, and reported success. Emit-and-route is the model dock-tiz describes - the agent says what it is looking at, Canvas decides whether and where to show it.

Transport already exists: stream.sock and StreamEnvelope (stream_binding.rs), the same path canvas-metrics uses. This is a new contract on it, something like canvas.agent.attention.v1 carrying { project, kind, target, region, at }.

What exists:
- media.rs handles PDF rasterization with MediaVariant::PdfPage { page_index },
  MediaPlan, MediaLimits and a resize-invalidating cache (media.rs:61-216).
- iced is already built with the highlighter and markdown features
  (crates/canvas/Cargo.toml:18), so syntax-highlighted code needs no new deps.

What does not exist:
- No region or bounding box. MediaVariant is page-level only, so 'show this
  section of page 4' needs a MediaVariant::PdfRegion { page_index, rect } and a
  crop in the plan.
- No code surface with a highlighted range. Showing a diff or an edited span
  needs a surface kind that takes { path, language, range } and scrolls to it.

Three things to get right or it becomes noise:
1. Salience and decay. An agent reads hundreds of files a minute; rendering
   every one strobes. Show what is notable - a write, a long read, a search hit
   - and let attention decay rather than clearing abruptly.
2. Privacy. This surfaces exactly what an agent is reading, which is the most
   sensitive thing on screen. Must respect dock-7pa sensitivity and presence:
   if it is not the owner watching, redact.
3. Per-project routing. This is the live counterpart to dock-aqz's red unread
   dot - one shows work happened, this shows work happening.
DESIGN REFINEMENT: a window per file, spatially clustered - not one window that jumps.

The principle: motion should be local, position should be stable. One surface following the agent around forces serial attention and strobes. A stable arrangement of per-file surfaces lets edits arrive serially but be taken in parallel, because the eye already knows where each file lives. Same reason a fixed dashboard beats a scrolling log.

Mechanics that follow:

- Surface identity is the file path, not the event. An edit routes to the
  existing surface for that file and highlights the changed range there. Events
  address surfaces by identity, so the same file always lands in the same place.
- A surface must not move when it updates. Only its content and highlight
  change. Position changes are reserved for a file entering or leaving the
  cluster, which is rare and therefore legible.
- New files claim a slot; the cluster grows and reflows around them. Existing
  surfaces keep their positions through that reflow wherever possible, because
  the whole value is that the anchor holds.
- Cold files decay and retire. Same LRU question as dock-aqz's project bar, and
  worth sharing one policy rather than inventing two.
- Cluster by project, since project is already the scoping unit for workspaces,
  backgrounds and views.

This makes the attention surface a view in the dock-blw sense: it reflows to
whatever displays exist, so one monitor shows a tight cluster of the few hottest
files and three monitors spread the working set out. layout_policy: reflow is
already the default and is exactly right here.

Salience then becomes about which files earn a slot, rather than which events
get drawn - a much easier question, and one that degrades gracefully: a file
that stops being touched simply fades out.
CAPACITY: a bounded working set with LRU, and resistance in both directions.

Roughly four surfaces at once, least-recently-used evicted when a new file claims a slot. Bounded so the cluster cannot overload; LRU so it keeps up with where the work actually is.

The trap is that plain LRU thrashes as soon as the hot set exceeds capacity. Bouncing between six files with four slots means they evict each other continuously, which reintroduces exactly the motion this design exists to avoid - strobing at slot granularity instead of window granularity. So resistance is needed on both edges:

- Admission resistance. A file earns a slot rather than taking one on first
  touch. A single read is not enough; a write, a repeat touch, or sustained
  attention is. This keeps an agent's incidental file-sniffing from evicting
  something the human is actually watching.
- Eviction hysteresis. A resident surface holds its slot for a minimum dwell
  time, so a brief detour cannot displace it. Recency alone is too twitchy at
  agent speeds, where dozens of files are touched per minute.
- Prefer evicting cold over evicting recent-but-brief, so a file touched once
  in passing loses to one being worked on steadily.

Capacity should be derived, not a constant (tenet 3). It follows available
display area: one monitor holds about four, three monitors hold proportionally
more, and it recomputes when displays change - which is dock-blw's reflow doing
the work. A constant would be wrong on both a laptop and a 5760px wall.

Shared with dock-aqz: the project launcher bar has the same admission and
eviction question for which projects stay pinned. One policy, two consumers.
STATUS 2026-09-10, verified: NOT STARTED. There is no canvas.agent.attention.v1 contract - the only
stream contracts that exist anywhere in the workspace are canvas.widget.snapshot.v1 and
canvas.quant.candle.v1. The "jarvis.attention.v2" string at crates/canvas/src/lib.rs:1582 is a
binding contract name inside a test, not an implementation. canvas-sse carries an "elmers/attention"
SOURCE ID in tests with the note "Elmer's exposes no attention stream yet" - which is honest and
still true.

ONE THING TO GET RIGHT WHEN THIS IS WRITTEN, cheaply, so it does not need a version bump later.
dock-qwv will give the stream retention and sequence assignment, and its recommended shape is
log-authoritative with screens projecting. This contract should therefore CARRY A SEQUENCE FROM DAY
ONE, even while nothing retains it and the value is always fresh.

Why it matters here specifically: attention is the payload people will most want to REWIND. "What
was the agent looking at when it made that change" is a question about a past position in the log,
and a contract without a sequence cannot answer it no matter what the backend later does. Adding the
field later means canvas.agent.attention.v2 and two live contracts to support.

So this bead can ship LOCALLY BEFORE dock-qwv exists - the transport is already there - as long as
the envelope is shaped for retention. That ordering is worth taking: attention is the most legible
demo on the wall and it does not need the backend to be useful on one machine.
CONCRETE PATH TO THE MILESTONE (Avery, 2026-09-10: "see the stuff the agent pulls" is the milestone
we are working towards). Status of each half, verified.

WHAT ALREADY WORKS TODAY: `canvas_open_file` is one of 19 MCP tools Canvas already exposes - "Open a
file (image, PDF, Markdown, or rendered Mermaid) as a Canvas surface." An agent can put what it is
reading on the wall RIGHT NOW, over MCP, with no new code.

WHY THAT IS NOT THE MILESTONE, and it sharpens this bead's own framing. The problem with
canvas_open_file is NOT that it is a tool call rather than a socket write - the emit/imperative
distinction has nothing to do with transport. It is about WHO DECIDES PLACEMENT. canvas_open_file
says "put this here"; the milestone needs "I am reading this", with Canvas deciding whether and
where. Nine agents calling canvas_open_file is the strobing wall this bead exists to prevent, and
each of them will report success.

SO THE CONTRACT IS THE WORK, and an MCP tool is the right way to carry it. Agents already speak MCP,
the registration already exists, and a tool gets schema and validation for free - whereas asking
every agent to write to stream.sock is a new transport for them to learn and no validation. Shape:
a `canvas_attention` tool taking { project, kind, target, region, at } that EMITS onto
canvas.agent.attention.v1 rather than mutating the document. Same transport as canvas_open_file, a
declarative contract instead of an imperative one.

WHAT IS NOT BLOCKED: this. The transport exists, StreamInbox now retains rather than drains, and
canvas_open_file already proves the file render path.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY MISSING, verified against the code:
- REGION. MediaVariant is page-level, so "show this section of page 4" needs MediaVariant::PdfRegion
  { page_index, rect } and a crop in the plan.
- CODE WITH A RANGE. `SurfaceContent` (lib.rs:337) has ProjectResource, Asset, Chart, Widget, Scene,
  Terminal, Stream - and nothing carrying { path, language, range }. Showing an edited span is a new
  variant, not a parameter on an existing one.
- ROUTING. Bounded working set, surfaces keyed by agent identity so updates route rather than
  create, and salience deciding which agents earn a slot. That half is dock-zqe's analysis and it
  applies here unchanged.

WHY THE LOG WORK WAS NOT A DETOUR: attention is the payload most worth rewinding - "what was the
agent looking at when it made that change" is a question about a past position - and the retained
log plus a held position is what makes that answerable. Emit the sequence in the contract from day
one, as noted above.

title: Canvas: presence-gated widget sensitivity (soft-lock instead of screen lock)
notes:
Widgets and artifacts carry a sensitivity. When presence says the viewer is not the owner - or that nobody is there - sensitive values degrade in place rather than the whole machine locking. Standing up should not require Windows+L, and someone walking past should not read the numbers.

The identity axis already exists: PresenceSignalState (crates/canvas/src/control.rs:362) distinguishes Unavailable, Unknown, Detected and Verified. Detected means a person is present; Verified means it is the owner. That is precisely the distinction this needs, and it is why JARVIS does identity at all.

Shape, following Provenance (docs/widget-quality.md rule 1) since this is the same family - a disclosure property alongside the data rather than inside it:

  enum Sensitivity { Public, Sensitive, EyesOnly }

Render policy:
  Verified              -> full detail
  Detected, not owner   -> Sensitive blurs values, EyesOnly redacts entirely
  Unknown / Unavailable -> treat as not-owner

That last line is the one that matters most: it must FAIL CLOSED. A camera that
is unplugged, a model that errors, a signal that has not arrived yet - all must
degrade to blurred, never to visible. The failure mode of the opposite choice is
that the privacy feature silently stops working and nothing on screen says so,
which is the same disclosure failure as an unmarked demo value.

Blur versus redaction is a real distinction, not a styling choice. A blurred
number still leaks magnitude and digit count, and blur is recoverable from a
photograph. Sensitive can blur; EyesOnly should replace with a block, not blur.

Also needs deciding:
- Hysteresis and a grace period. Flickering between Detected and Verified as
  someone shifts in their chair must not strobe the dashboard. Debounce, and
  bias toward staying degraded once degraded.
- Whether degrading is announced. A visible 'privacy active' marker is honest
  and reassuring; it also tells an onlooker there is something worth hiding.
- Existing related work: commit bd6180e feat(canvas): presence-aware privacy
  screensaver already blanks on absence. This is the finer-grained,
  per-widget version, and the two should share one policy rather than
  disagreeing about what absence means.

title: canvas-widgets: project launcher bar with unread indicators
notes:
A horizontal bar of small project tiles across the top of the home view. Each tile is an icon or logo, clicking it jumps to that project, and a red dot marks a project with an unread update or briefing.

Ordering should be dynamic rather than a hand-maintained list - recency (LRU) or frequency, possibly with pinned favourites ahead of the dynamic tail. Ordering rule is undecided; LRU is the obvious first cut and is cheap to change once it is being used daily.

Three dependencies worth naming:

1. Click-to-jump is the same interaction contract dock-4s7 (RSS reader) needs.
   Widgets are presentation-only today; nothing in the library performs an
   action. Both widgets want a host-mediated activation, not a raw call from
   inside the widget. Whichever lands first should define it.

2. Per docs/widget-quality.md rule 5 the widget must not discover projects or
   poll for unread state itself. Project identity belongs to Alfalfa (the
   dock-workspaces MCP already exposes projects_list and project_recall), and
   unreads belong to whatever owns briefings. The widget receives a payload of
   { project_id, label, icon, unread: bool, last_used }.

3. Icons are the first asset-bearing widget. media.rs already handles image
   assets with caching and resize invalidation, so the tiles should reuse that
   rather than grow their own path.

Shape-wise this is close to a generic 'tile strip' - labelled, iconned,
selectable items with a badge - so per rule 4 it should probably be named for
that shape rather than for projects, and the home view supplies the projects.

title: Canvas: Ctrl-O jumps back through navigation history
notes:
Ctrl-O returns to the previous location, in the vim jump-list sense: the place you were before the last jump, not an undo of document edits.

What counts as a jump needs deciding before implementing, because the wrong granularity makes the key useless:
- project switch (Ctrl-P, workspace_activate)
- operational view activation (view <project/view>)
- display target change (Ctrl-1/2/3/0)
- surface focus change

My read: the first two are jumps, the last two are not. Changing which monitors Canvas occupies is not somewhere you 'were', and focus changes are far too frequent to be worth a history entry - a jump list that fills with focus changes is one you can never navigate out of.

Pairs naturally with Ctrl-I to jump forward, and with the existing Ctrl-Option-L snap/restore, which is already a two-state peek. Worth checking they do not feel redundant: snap restores a layout, this restores a location.

Existing state to build on: snapped_view already tracks the active view id, and workspace_store.rs has activate(). Neither keeps history.
close_reason: Closed

title: Widget artifacts: bind query, binder and widget into one addressable unit
notes:
Per docs/widget-quality.md, the artifact model. A query, a mapping and a presentation only work when they agree, but today they live in three unrelated files with no manifest and no resolution order:

  config/metrics.json    the query
  config/binders/*.lua   the mapping
  canvas-widgets         the presentation

Package them:

  artifacts/<id>/manifest.json   id, version, widget kind, source binding, provenance
  artifacts/<id>/binder.lua      the mapping, sandboxed and bounded as binders already are

Resolution project first, then global, then built-in, so a project can override a shared artifact without forking it.

The machinery mostly exists: apply_named_adapter already loads named Lua binders from config/binders with a 32KB source cap and 256-event batches. What is missing is the manifest, the resolution order, and enforcing the quality bar once at the artifact boundary rather than per widget.

title: canvas-widgets: widgets must not source their own data
notes:
Per docs/widget-quality.md rule 5. Anything a widget can fetch, it can fetch at the wrong time, in the wrong order, with credentials it should not hold.

Violations:
- Chart { source: PathBuf } holds a filesystem path. The chart data should arrive as a payload like every other widget, resolved by whoever owns the file.
- Ticker { symbols } carries identifiers it resolves to values itself (see the mock_price bug).
- Clock { format } reads the system clock. Intrinsic rather than sourced, and the one defensible exception; document it as such rather than fixing it.

Enforceable: canvas-widgets should not depend on std::fs, reqwest, or a clock.
close_reason: Closed

title: Prototype a Manim-style explanatory animation backend for Canvas
description: Prototype a native Canvas animation scene layer inspired by 3Blue1Brown's Manim so an agent can turn typed data plus bounded scene logic into clear mathematical, engineering, and briefing animations during a session.
design: Do not embed arbitrary Python execution in the renderer. Define a renderer-neutral retained animation scene with timeline, camera, text/math, paths, plots, transforms, annotations and deterministic playback. Evaluate whether Manim assets/semantics can be imported or called through an isolated artifact pipeline while Canvas owns the live GPU compositor. Lua may bind typed data and declared transitions within budgets.
acceptance_criteria: A design spike compares direct Manim artifact import with a native retained scene; one typed dataset produces a deterministic animated explanation with seek/pause/replay and shared human-agent selection; generated assets carry provenance; malformed or over-budget scenes fail visibly; licensing, font/math, export, and GPU performance constraints are recorded before choosing an integration.

title: Build a privacy-aware contact and personnel card widget
description: Add a reusable Canvas contact/personnel-file widget for quickly bringing up a person with a portrait, preferred identity, roles and organizations, safe contact methods, relationship context, recent verified facts, provenance, freshness, and owner-app deep links. The widget is read-only; connectors own access policy and redact sensitive fields before Canvas receives typed data.
design: Use the shared Coherence WidgetFrame with compact and expanded layouts. Keep portrait/media identity separate from contact/fact records. Facts carry source and observed/verified time; stale, missing, conflicting, and redacted values are explicit. Never persist credentials or fields outside the connector's declared projection.
acceptance_criteria: A typed bounded contact spec renders compact and expanded fixtures in light/dark/project themes; portrait fallback, long names, multiple roles, stale facts, redaction, missing data, and source provenance are visually verified; data validation rejects oversized/untrusted content; one fixture composes into a named read-only view without source-specific rendering code.

title: Consolidate the Lua activity graph input worktree
description: The activity-graph subagent left useful uncommitted GraphSnapshot/Lua module work in feat/activity-graph-input. Move the typed graph contract and example module onto current master, add the missing bounded validation and tests, then retire the worktree without merging the stale dock-refactor branch.

Removed the now-redundant feat/activity-graph-input worktree and branch. refactor/module-extraction remains deliberately unmerged because it is the stale dock-refactor architecture that duplicates newer surface/chart/view models.

title: Repair the broken Widgets Demo tab
description: The existing Widgets Demo tab has remained broken across multiple Canvas iterations. Reproduce the current failure, identify whether the stale tab points at missing decoded scene/widget state or broken stack selection, and repair it without introducing a second demo-only rendering path.
acceptance_criteria: Opening and selecting Widgets Demo visibly renders its configured widget instances; switching away and back preserves them; focus, close, minimize/restore, workspace save/recall, and Canvas restart do not leave a blank or stale tab; a regression test exercises the production widget/stack path.
notes: 2026-09-08 root cause confirmed from live screenshot: OpenWidget rendered only in decoded runtime and persisted a fake ProjectResource, so validation/save/restart could not reconstruct it. Current fix adds durable SurfaceContent::Widget, production renderer rehydration, MCP canvas_open_widget + canvas_workspace_save, five validated demo specs, and a workspace-store/restart regression test. target now links to warm shared cache /Volumes/DockBuild/dock-target; normal Cargo profile required to reuse it.

title: Register new widget kinds over MCP, committed on create, never blocking
description:
Depends on dock-cov.9. The flow: an agent meets a shape the vocabulary does not have, writes a Lua module defining a new widget kind, registers it over MCP, and it is usable in the same session. No build step - Luau needs no compile, so check-in to live is near-instant.

Two MCP surfaces, not one, because they carry different risk:
- create/modify an INSTANCE is data. Free, no commit, no review.
- create/modify a KIND is code. Committed on create, rate-limited.

Committing on create is for durability and corpus, not approval. Nothing that an agent authored should exist only inside a session, and a vocabulary that cannot be read all at once cannot later be consolidated. The git history doubles as the record dock-cov.11 works against.

Never block in the flow. Registration must not wait on a human; that is a review gate and tenet 9 already says what those cost.

Reframes the constraint in docs/canvas-mcp.md that MCP tools 'do not execute Lua, shell commands, or launch applications': this is not executing caller-supplied code on demand, it is registering a definition the host validates, sandboxes and versions. Same sandbox as any other module - fresh VM per invocation, no filesystem, network, process, package, clock or GPU access, with memory, interrupt, source and node ceilings.

Make finding cheaper than making: the tool should surface matching existing kinds before it will create one. fpl-skills discovery and elmers capability_catalog.rs are the two precedents in the estate.

title: Widget library crate: reusable presentation primitives
description: Extract widget primitives (clock, ticker, gauge/VU, chart, status orb) from dock-canvas into a dock-widgets crate. WidgetSpec JSON model drives two backends: live iced-native rendering (in-canvas surfaces) and static PNG via external tools (doc-forge for HTML/CSS widgets, plotters/matplotlib for charts — same pattern as mermaid/.mmd → mmdc → PNG). Lua module + MCP tool + text protocol all become thin clients of the library.

Two backends: live iced-native (live::element for all kinds, ChartProgram for charts) and static PNG via external tools (render.rs delegates to matplotlib via python3, plotters helper fallback — same pattern as mermaid/mmdc). title: Add configurable compact presence orb and audio meters

Support an LED-segment meter and a classic VU treatment as selectable themes. title: Rotating shader screensaver background with attribution
description: Canvas bottom-layer animated background: rotate through a curated set of fragment-shader pieces (Shadertoy or equivalent sources) every ~45s. Each piece carries a manifest entry: title, author, source URL, and the license detected from the source page at curation time; attribution renders in the lower-left corner (e.g. 'Title — Author (License)'). CPU-rendered at background resolution (iced image widget) so it runs identically on Mac and the GTX node; no GPU dependency. Only include sources whose license permits use with attribution; never assume.

Stopped target/debug/dock-canvas and restored stable ~/.local/bin/dock-canvas on the right monitor. Shader generation must remain opt-in until dock-q26.21-style pacing work is verified. Current architecture creates a new iced image handle after synchronous GPU readback; measure it and replace or contain that path before enabling by default.
2026-09-07 correction: the synchronous GPU-to-CPU readback and per-frame iced image allocation were removed after severe live flicker. The active renderer is now an iced-native retained GPU primitive. Animation defaults off, is socket-controlled, validates a 1-60 FPS bound, and exposes optional measured/target FPS. Shader WGSL is parsed in tests before live pipeline creation; malformed Spirales/Floating Rectangles/Smoke Rings ports were caught and corrected. Live managed binary is stable on the right display at 14.88-15.01 measured FPS for a 15 FPS target.

title: Canvas surface placement ignores normalized bounds (centering wins)
description: In dock-canvas view(), each surface plane is .center(Length::Fill) inside a full-frame container whose padding is the bounds offset. The padding only shrinks the centering region, so surfaces render centered in (W-x, H-y) instead of at (bounds.x, bounds.y) — verified live: a surface placed at x:0.05,y:0.12 rendered with image center ~x:0.5,y:0.57 of the frame. Normalized placements therefore only shift where the surface drifts to, they do not position it. Fix: drop the centering so the padded top-left anchor positions the plane (or compute an explicit offset). Blocks accurate workspace recall and makes swap animations land on wrong targets.
close_reason: Closed

title: Add presence-aware privacy screensaver scenes to Canvas

than six months is stale, so "no, permanently" would be as wrong as "yes, now". This is a QUARTERLY
MEASUREMENT against wpt.servo.org/scores.json, with thresholds fixed in advance so the re-check is a
measurement and not an argument.

  Agent browsing viable   silent-failure fraction below 3%      today 11.4%
     (harness tests Chrome passes that Servo fails with status `O` - not the headline score; this is
      the number that makes an agent report confident nonsense)
  Attention display       reftest parity above 90%              today 66.4%
     (below that the human is checking the renderer, not the agent)
  AX driving viable       /accname/ above 80%                   today 0.0%

Full reasoning and every measurement in docs/servo-and-web-surfaces-decision.md. The numbers above

title: canvas-widgets: the OKLCH gamut map runs in tests but nothing asserts it holds hue
notes:
The OKLCH gamut map (live.rs:1128-1215) reduces chroma by bisection instead of clipping RGB
channels, specifically so that an out-of-gamut colour keeps its hue. The doc comment at live.rs:1155
claims the naive clip shifts hue by about 14 degrees. That number has no test behind it.

TWO EARLIER CLAIMS ABOUT THIS WERE BOTH WRONG, which is why it is worth writing down:
- "the bisection has zero coverage" - FALSE. `from_oklch` is reached from `series_colors`
  (live.rs:1028) and from the stale drain (:767), and series_colors is exercised by four tests
  (2184, 2211, 2228, 2242). At SERIES_LIGHTNESS_MAX 0.92 with SERIES_CHROMA_MAX 0.15 the branch does
  fire, so those tests already run it.
- "covered by a test at 2129 asserting chroma retention" - also FALSE. live.rs:2126-2131 asserts
  `drained.c < live.c`, which is chroma REDUCTION on the stale path, not the gamut map.

So the loop is executed but nothing ASSERTS ITS BEHAVIOUR. A regression that silently started
clipping would still pass `series_colours_stay_apart_from_each_other`.

WORK, about 15 lines: construct a deliberately out-of-gamut Oklch, assert `from_oklch` holds hue
within tolerance while reducing chroma, and assert the naive channel-clip alternative shifts hue
measurably. That turns the 14-degree prose claim into a fact and hardens the most carefully-reasoned
code in the repo.

title: Canvas: render web content in a surface via a Rust engine, not a bundled Chromium
notes:
Show HTML content inside a Canvas surface - RSS article bodies (dock-4s7), documents, briefings, rendered reports - without bundling Chromium or depending on Playwright.

Nothing web-related exists in the tree today: no servo, wry, webview, blitz or cef in any Cargo.toml. platform::open_url (main.rs:6637) shells out to the system browser, and rich text is iced's markdown + highlighter features.

WHY THE EASY OPTION IS WRONG HERE. A system webview - wry/WKWebView, what Tauri
uses - is the lightest general answer and the wrong one for Canvas. It is a
native WINDOW, not a texture. Canvas composites surfaces into a wgpu scene, so a
native view cannot be composited, cannot be captured for a remote screen
(dock-qwv), and cannot exist in the WASM tier (dock-8nz). The architecture rules
it out even though it would be cheapest elsewhere.

That leaves two, and the choice turns on whether JavaScript is needed:

- BLITZ - Stylo (Servo's CSS engine) plus a wgpu renderer, HTML and CSS with no
  JS engine. Renders to a texture, which is exactly Canvas's model. Far smaller
  dependency and attack surface.
- SERVO (libservo) - the full engine including SpiderMonkey. Real web apps.
  Heavier, and its embedding API is the thing to verify rather than assume.

RECOMMENDATION: Blitz-class first. The listed uses are documents and article
bodies, not web applications, and a JS engine is a much larger attack surface to
place next to a sensitive dashboard. Reach for full Servo only when something
genuinely needs to RUN rather than be READ.

VERIFY BEFORE COMMITTING - a spike, not a decision from memory:
1. Does the candidate render into a wgpu texture Canvas can composite, or does
   it insist on owning a surface or window?
2. Does it build for the platforms Canvas targets, and at what compile cost?
   This machine already takes 12-15 minutes for a cold canvas build.
3. What is the failure mode on content it cannot render? Per
   docs/widget-quality.md rule 3 it must say so rather than showing a blank
   surface that reads as broken.

DESIGN CONSTRAINTS:
- The WASM tier does not need this. In a browser you would use an iframe, so the
  two LoD tiers render web content by different means. That asymmetry is fine
  but should be explicit rather than discovered.
- Untrusted content sits next to sensitive surfaces, so dock-7pa sensitivity and
  presence gating apply to a web surface like any other - arguably more.
- Per rule 5 the widget must not fetch. Whatever fetches the page is a source
  that hands the surface bytes, the same split as every other connector.

title: Canvas backgrounds: reduce shader cost without frame caching
notes:
Question raised 2026-09-09: since backgrounds are loops, can a loop be cached after one pass until the speed changes?

Mostly they are not loops. Reading how time enters each shader in crates/canvas/src/screensaver.rs:

Never repeats - time translates through a field rather than driving a phase:
- STAR_NEST: ray_origin = base + vec3(time*2, time, -2), flying through a
  fractal indefinitely
- MEME: m_noise(p * 5.0 + time)
- SMOKE_RINGS, FLOATING_RECT: fbm/noise driven by t

Possibly periodic - time enters through sin/cos: TIDEPOOL, AURORA_DRIFT,
DUSK_EMBER, SLOW_RIPPLE, SPIRAL, FLAME. These repeat only if every
time-dependent frequency is commensurable; mixing sin(t) with sin(1.7t) gives
a quasi-periodic result that looks like a loop and never exactly repeats. Each
would need per-shader frequency analysis to find a period, if one exists.

Caching is the expensive option regardless. At 5760x1200 one frame is 27.6 MB;
a 2 second loop at 30 fps is 1.66 GB of VRAM, and blitting that costs more
memory bandwidth per frame than re-running most of these shaders.

Cheaper levers, in order of value:
1. Lower max_fps for backgrounds. FrameClock already supports this
   (screensaver.rs:672 interval() = 1/max_fps, set_max_fps at :676) and tests
   run it at 50 ms. Backgrounds are low-frequency motion; 20-24 fps is
   usually indistinguishable from 60 and is a direct linear saving.
2. Render at reduced resolution and upscale. These shaders are low spatial
   frequency, so half-res is typically invisible and costs a quarter of the
   fragment work. Star Nest is the exception, with fine star detail that
   aliases when downsampled.
3. Skip entirely when Canvas is hidden or fully occluded. Cheapest of all
   because it costs nothing when it does not apply.

Only worth doing if backgrounds actually show up in a profile; measure first.
close_reason: Closed

title: canvas-widgets: RSS reader widget with click-to-open
notes:
Deferred - on the shopping list, not queued.

A feed-reading widget: entries with title, source, timestamp, and a link that opens in the browser when clicked.

Two things make this more than another list widget, and both should be settled before building it:

1. Per docs/widget-quality.md rule 5, the widget must not fetch the feed. RSS
   polling, parsing, and caching belong to a source that hands the widget a
   payload, the same way canvas-metrics does for Prometheus. The widget kind is
   then close to a shape that already exists - a list of { title, source,
   timestamp, url } is EventEntry with a link.

2. Click-to-open is a genuinely new capability. Widgets are presentation only
   today; nothing in the library performs an action. Opening a URL means an
   interaction contract, and a widget that can open a browser can be pointed at
   a URL that arrived over a stream - so the opening should be host-mediated
   with the URL scheme constrained, not a raw open() from the widget.

Likely lands after the artifact model, since a feed source plus binder plus
widget is exactly one artifact.

title: Keep the visual vocabulary converging as it expands
description:
Deliberately later. Recorded now so the reasoning is not lost, because the decisions in dock-cov.9 and dock-cov.10 are what make it possible or impossible.

The goal is a visual language that can expand without sprawling: coining a new widget kind stays free and instant, and something pulls the vocabulary back toward a consistent core over time. Not a gate. Blocking coinage in the flow is exactly the scaling liability tenet 9 warns about, and the flow is the product.

Coherence already solved this one layer down: module.theme exposes semantic colors and metrics so Lua 'receives semantic colors and metrics without owning or duplicating a palette'. Nobody is stopped from choosing a color, the choice simply is not reachable. Core widget kinds are the same idea at the vocabulary layer.

Four pressures, none blocking:
- Measure use, not intent. A kind used once six weeks ago is an absorption candidate; one used widely has earned promotion. Instances being data makes this countable.
- Make the core the path of least resistance. Search-before-create answering 'this exists and is 90 percent of it' converges by ergonomics.
- Detect duplicates structurally. Manifests declare inputs, so two kinds with the same input shape and similar scene output are mechanically comparable. A name-only registry can never tell you this.
- Give promotion a place to live. Two tiers: coined is free and instant, core is deliberate and rare, so the consolidation conversation has a home instead of being a recurring nag.

The trigger matters more than the mechanism. 'Consolidate later' with nothing surfacing it is the same as no plan. Cheapest durable version is a periodic report over the corpus - kinds by usage, kinds unused since coined, pairs with matching input shapes - somewhere it will actually be seen.

title: Maximize animations
description: Animated maximize/restore transitions for canvas surfaces. When a surface is maximized (fills display) or restored (returns to previous bounds), animate the bounds change. Should integrate with the drag-to-move feature and workspace switching. Consider staggered animation when multiple surfaces are involved.
close_reason: Closed

title: Animations for swaps/movements
description: Smooth animation transitions when surfaces swap positions, move, or are resized. The iced framework supports implicit animations via animated values. Need to interpolate Layout/Placement bounds and surface geometry over ~200-300ms, with easing (ease-out for movement). Animation state should be tracked in App and driven by the Tick subscription.
notes:
Canvas snapshots pre-change placement and palette state and interpolates presentation-only bounds/colors for 280ms with cubic ease-out. ApplyDocument, ApplyPatch, and SetTheme trigger transitions; logical state and socket receipts remain immediate. Tick cadence rises to 16ms only while animated. Unit tests cover endpoints, bounds, palette roles, completion, and new-surface behavior.
Transition engine implemented + verified live (2026-09-07):
- New crates/dock-canvas/src/transition.rs: ease-out-cubic, lerp/lerp_rgb/lerp_palette, Transition{started, duration=280ms, from_placements, from_palette}; 5 unit tests (easing shape, lerp bounds, all-role palette lerp, finish/snap, new-surface snap).
- App wiring in main.rs: transition field; start_transition() called before mutation in ApplyDocument/ApplyPatch/SetTheme; presented_palette()/presented_bounds() helpers; tick_transition() on Tick; subscription cadence 16ms while transition in flight.
- Design holds: logical state applies instantly (revision bumps synchronously, input never locked), presentation interpolates. A dropped transition snaps to target.
- LIVE PROOF (window 20599, 2 surfaces, swap A->B): mid frame captured 207ms after swap sits strictly between before and after for both surfaces — red (964,676)->(1478,747)->(1554,877), blue (1510,690)->(1242,798)->(1030,885). Animation confirmed.
RECONNECT NEEDED (main.rs is mid-refactor by the module-extraction work, dock-q26.14 — the view call sites were dropped in that refactor and the tree is currently red for unrelated in-flight reasons):
1. view(): use self.presented_palette() instead of self.project_theme().palette() (background gradient, surface/border/text colors, theme(), title bar).
2. Canvas branch: build bounds from self.presented_bounds(&placement.surface_id, placement.bounds) instead of placement.bounds directly (maximized surfaces keep snapping).
Also discovered: dock-q26.16 — placement bug (centering wins over bounds) means swap targets are wrong until fixed; animation math itself is verified correct.
close_reason: Closed

title: First-class palette import: theme files and ricer format adapters
description: Stop deriving all visuals from the two Coherence modes only. Make ThemePalette (dock-core) the canonical theme boundary and import palettes as first-class inputs. Design: (1) A 'Dock theme file' JSON format mapping canonical roles (background, background_strong, surface, surface_muted, text, text_muted, primary, success, warning, danger, info, border, border_strong) to hex colors. (2) Adapters for common ricer palette formats - catppuccin JSON, tokyo-night JSON, nord, gruvbox toml - mapping their role names onto canonical roles. (3) Missing roles are DERIVED by transform (shade/tint/alpha of a base role), computed not configured. (4) Per-project theme source becomes an enum: coherence mode OR imported theme file; generalize the existing per-project theme files (dock-linux theme_path: dock.conf / <project>.conf). (5) Dock never re-exports Coherence values; imported themes coexist with Coherence as a theme source.
design: Universal denominator across catppuccin/tokyo-night/rose-pine/nord/gruvbox/dracula: base bg, one darker layer, one lighter surface, text, muted text, 1 accent, optional red/green/yellow/blue semantics, border. ThemePalette roles cover all of that. Keep adapters boring: one struct per format, explicit field mapping, fail loud on missing required roles that cannot be derived.
notes: Implemented canonical ThemePalette imports for Dock JSON, Catppuccin JSON, Tokyo Night JSON, Nord TOML, and Gruvbox TOML with deterministic derived roles and strict validation. Canvas now consumes ThemePalette directly, including imported projects, with a runtime regression test. Workspace all-feature tests and strict Clippy pass.
close_reason: Palette import adapters, canonical theme boundary, consumer integration, and tests are complete.

title: Rice capture: composite all displays into one annotated screenshot
description: The r/unixporn feature: a dockctl command that composites every connected display's Canvas surface into a single multi-screen screenshot, optionally annotated (project name, timestamp), ready to post. Reuse existing per-surface media plans and display frame metadata in Canvas; new CLI path in dockctl. Output to a caller-chosen path, deterministic layout from the display topology.

title: Window decoration: rounded canvas surfaces, accent borders, focus animation
description: Sway uses flat 'client.focused #fff...' colors with plain gaps. Add the Hyprland-style drama: rounded corners on Canvas surfaces, per-project accent border color derived from ProjectTheme, and an animated border/focus transition when the project changes. Sway side: per-project client border colors and gap values in the generated config; Canvas side: surface frame styling in view(). Coherence palette throughout.

title: Wallpaper upgrades: gradient, dim-on-focus, per-project wallpaper
description: Sway plan currently only does 'output * bg #18191c solid_color' (crates/dock-linux/src/desktop.rs:804). Extend WallpaperRequest/Wallpaper enum to support gradient backgrounds and dim-on-focus. Per-project wallpaper already half-exists via WallpaperRequest; complete it so each project recall can carry its own backdrop.

title: Load proper mono font and fix hardcoded FPL chip color
description: Canvas renders everything in iced's default font. Load a real mono (Iosevka or JetBrains Mono) via Font::try_load. Also the FPL chip at crates/dock-canvas/src/main.rs:1092 hardcodes white text/border instead of using the Coherence palette from ProjectTheme. Wire the chip to the project theme.

title: Implement stable Windows desktop helper adapter
description: Implement the dock-core window, wallpaper, and supported workspace contracts in an independently installed Windows helper. Preserve helper identity and permissions across ordinary Dock GUI rebuilds; use a same-user authenticated local IPC channel and public Windows APIs for inventory, focus, geometry, display wallpaper, and any workspace operations that can be verified.
design: Mirror the Dock Control process boundary rather than sharing macOS implementation details. The orchestrator sends typed dock-core requests without PowerShell, registry, or shell payloads. Use Windows UI Automation/window APIs and per-monitor wallpaper APIs behind bounded operations, explicit capabilities, stale-window detection, and apply receipts. Keep future compositor/backend selection outside Alfalfa.
acceptance_criteria: A separately installed Windows helper implements the applicable dock-core traits over same-user local IPC, changes only explicitly bound windows/displays, survives GUI rebuilds without permission identity churn, rejects stale or ambiguous handles, and returns verified receipts. Unit tests cover protocol validation and deterministic layout projection; a live Windows run proves focus, frame, restore, and per-display wallpaper behavior.

title: Evaluate Browser MCP for project-scoped browser control on Mac and Agora
description: Run a bounded later-stage spike of BrowserMCP/mcp as a client of each machine's existing authenticated browser profile. Determine whether it can replace or complement Dock's narrow browser operations without copying cookies, crossing project profiles, bypassing the agent-control gate, or exposing its browser-control socket beyond the local machine. Test Mac and Agora independently; Agora currently uses persistent Firefox profiles, while Browser MCP requires a Chrome extension. Treat the published package as the candidate because the public repository states it cannot build standalone.
design: Keep the MCP server and extension colocated with the browser they control. Do not forward Browser MCP's WebSocket port through Dock or expose it on LAN/Tailscale. OpenCode/Edgerunner remains the MCP client owner; Dock supplies project identity and existing human-takeover authorization. Pin a reviewed version and extension identity for any spike. Compare against the current dock-linux browser API and call the existing owner instead of duplicating automation logic.
acceptance_criteria: Document the published server and extension versions tested; verify actual listen address and whether the extension/server channel authenticates; reject any default 0.0.0.0 or unauthenticated control path unless isolated by a maintained upstream configuration; prove a browser action only in an explicitly attached project profile on Mac and Agora; verify another project/profile cannot be read or controlled; verify human takeover revokes agent browser operations; measure idle and repeated-action memory; preserve browser login across restart without exporting cookies; compare reliability and tool surface with Dock's current browser operations; record an adopt, wrap, or reject decision and remove all spike services/extensions if rejected.

title: Prototype custom compositing client after exhausting stock remoting
description: Mesh §§3,8 long-term. Evaluate moonlight-common-c decode and ScreenCaptureKit capture for local/remote texture compositing. Preserve transport/core boundary and only use opaque video when structural access is unavailable. Acceptance: benchmark against working stock Sunshine/Moonlight before replacement.

title: Replace Sway backend with Smithay after core daily-use validation
description: Mesh §§2,7,8. Future phase only after Mac AX and pane interfaces prove stable. Implement the same backend contract using Smithay without changing upstream profile or orchestration semantics. Acceptance: backend contract and daily-use parity tests.

title: Build session gateway with structural pane access and existing identity
description: Mesh §§3–5,8. Expose background agents as PTY/structural panes, reuse Tailscale and FPL OIDC, support PTY convergence and CDP/AX structural access. Keep opaque streaming on demand and Shroud GPU-free. Acceptance: authenticated local/remote panes share addressing and reconnect semantics.
notes: User identifies Edge Runner as long-term owner/host for OpenCode sessions, with Codex/Claude sessions potentially on Agora One. Investigate actual existing session interfaces before designing adapters. Desired capability: agent and human can locate, manage and prompt sessions through project workspace orchestration, with explicit takeover and lifecycle behavior.

title: Resolve session locality, persistence, dispatch and shared-node identity
description: Mesh §9. Decide per-VM versus pooled session gateway, Shroud suspend/resume versus reopen-on-boot, dispatch_task relationship, and multi-person node arbitration. Record decisions in Beads before implementing affected contracts.

title: Formalize profile contract and connect JARVIS tier-1 activation
description: Mesh §§2,5,8. Migrate proven v0 profile format to the real core, keeping executors replaceable. Call the existing JARVIS deterministic tier-1 action owner; do not rebuild agency. Acceptance: voice and UI activate identical profiles through the same interface.

title: Implement pane-tree layout core and public macOS AX backend
description: Mesh §§2,7,8 phase Next. Define PTY/CDP/AX/opaque handles and pure layout-to-rectangles interface; implement toggleable AX move/resize/focus/observe without SIP-gated APIs. Acceptance: deterministic layout tests and daily-driver Mac validation, with no transport or compute internals in the core.
notes: User expanded the backend requirement on 2026-09-07: keep one typed core contract across macOS helper, Windows helper, Sway, and future compositors. Initial dock-core WindowBackend/WorkspaceBackend/WallpaperBackend and deterministic browser-primary geometry moved into active v0 work dock-96j.34.1. This later pane-tree task retains structural PTY/CDP/AX/opaque handle work beyond that v0 surface.

title: Computing mesh after Dock v0: orchestration and session roadmap
description: Architectural reference and conditional future candidates from computing-mesh design, not an approved build queue. First learn from a usable Linux desktop streamed to Mac. Existing JARVIS, Shroud, Tailscale, OIDC and Coherence remain owned externally; only demonstrated integration gaps belong here. Reassess pane core, profile formalization, session gateway, compositor and custom client against current implementations before scheduling.

title: Resolve long-term profile and Coherence artifact ownership
description: First-cut §7. Initial boundary: vendored upstream token JSON produces shared runtime JSON plus Waybar CSS. Decide refresh ownership and profile location with Coherence; reserve JARVIS integration contract without implementing agency.

title: Surface microinteractions: enter/exit slides, hover, focus fade
description: Low-priority polish pass on Canvas iced rendering: surfaces slide/fade in and out on placement changes, hover states on interactive regions, and a focus-fade when switching projects. Timer-subscription-driven, no control protocol changes. Should ride on the same animation infrastructure as dock-96j.39 (animated indicators).

title: Evaluate captured-reality splats as a domain-composition example (later)
description:
## Context
2026-09-07 user direction: bead and defer Gaussian splatting. It illustrates domain management, not a new near-term graphics priority. Related to Canvas dock-2kf.9, but explicitly outside initial Canvas acceptance.

## Deferred experiment
After durable artifact bundles and initial Canvas are usable, evaluate one eShelf capture/splat aligned with authoritative CAD and one legion-of-bom component annotation. Preserve capture inputs/calibration, selected reconstruction masters, tool versions and provenance. Distinguish as-observed timestamps/alignment uncertainty from as-designed dimensions. Precision operations resolve through domain-qualified geometry, not visual splats. Stream versioned spatial chunks/LODs with bounded CPU/GPU caches; cache eviction never deletes the only preserved copy. Benchmark stereo tail frame times against 90-120 Hz targets; no automatic performance claim. MIT-only implementation/dependency qualification before adoption; Spark is an evaluation reference, not a native wgpu commitment.

## Domain model illustrated
Broad systems (Transmog/manufacturing, legion-of-bom/ECE) and focused tools (Wideline/conversion telemetry, Meridian/ad management and creative assets) participate through narrow versioned capability contracts. Breadth does not determine integration privilege, deployment topology or require a universal internal schema. Domain owners retain semantics, validation, queries and mutation policy; shared storage owns durable authorized bytes/versions/protection; Canvas owns presentation; memory consumes authorized provenance-backed projections. A project can span domains; domain membership or linking is not an access grant. No new service per domain by default.

## References
shared-infra/docs/storage-substrate.md sections 13-15.
ads/wideline/README.md; ads/meridian/README.md; ads/wideline/wideline-meridian-L0-contract.md (design history, not proof every gate is implemented).
https://github.com/sparkjsdev/spark
https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.12080
acceptance_criteria: When explicitly resumed: demonstrate a portable versioned capture/CAD/BOM bundle, authorized cross-domain references, truthful precision vs appearance, preserved source/master recovery after cache eviction, and measured cold/warm and stereo rendering budgets. Document narrow adapter ownership and MIT license qualification. Not a blocker or closure requirement for initial Canvas or memory ingestion.
notes: Explicit user deferral: domain-model illustration, not current delivery work; revisit only when intentionally scheduled.
